10755-the-broken-road:
A. E. W. Mason, author of The Four Feathers, published The Broken Road in 1907, a novel of British India and the frontier. Its chapters run from the breaking of a road and Linforth's death through a fort, Lahore, the polo-ground, Peshawar, and the claims of Chiltistan on Shere Ali. Luffe, Sybil Linforth, and Mrs. Oliver move through the tale.

Mason writes of duty, loyalty, and empire on the Northwest Frontier, where roads, regiments, and local princes shape men's fates. The story mixes romance with adventure in high places. Readers get a stirring imperial novel, with India itself as a living presence.
119-a-tramp-abroad:
Mark Twain promised a walking tour of Europe and delivered jokes, detours, and tall tales. A Tramp Abroad, first published in 1880, follows Twain and his agent Harris from Hamburg through Heidelberg and the Alps. The pair mostly ride, float, and argue instead of walking.

Chapters mock German student duels, beer halls, castles, and guides with deadpan invention. Jim Baker's tale of a blue jay and the ascent of the Riffelberg stand out. Illustrations from the first edition add to the comedy. The book remains a favorite of Twain's travel humor.
12630-the-adventures-of-old-mr-toad:
Thornton W. Burgess's 1920 animal tale, illustrated by Harrison Cady, follows Old Mr. Toad around the Smiling Pool. Jimmy Skunk is puzzled, consults friends and hunts for the toad, while Peter Rabbit finds him, discovers his music bag and more, and watches a shadow pass over the pool.

Toad's babies, a kindergarten, little toads starting out to see the world, a queer tongue shown and hidden, a scare for Peter, a full stomach, puffed pride and a lesson learned follow. Burgess writes gentle nature stories for children, mixing fact about toads with fable. The book is a charming woodland tale, teaching kindness and humility through animal neighbours.
13679-andrew-the-glad:
Maria Thompson Daviess published this 1913 novel about Andrew Sevier, a young man known for his glad spirit. The story opens with Major Matilda's circle brewing mystery from simple lives. Andrew moves among Kentucky neighbours, old soldiers, and young women with secrets. Chapters follow a heart trap, a ritual, small crimes, and a bridge of dreams.

Daviess writes in a warm Southern voice, with humour and sentiment in equal measure. Andrew's cheerfulness steadies friends in trouble and softens old quarrels. Romance grows slowly, tested by pride and misunderstanding. The novel closes with love and home after long wandering. It is a pleasant period romance, rich in local colour and talk.
13816-the-jericho-road:
W. Bion Adkins wrote The Jericho Road in 1901 as a tribute to Odd-Fellowship. He compares the order to rivers forever running yet never passed, and winds forever going yet never gone. Dedication addresses worthy and gentle brothers, hoping the book spurs greater effort for the order. Poems and prose praise strong minds, great hearts, and ready hands.

Adkins argues that union adds strength to kind words, cheer, and consolation. Friendly help and tender care, joined in God's work, form the order's life-giving principle. The book mixes devotion, fraternal history, and moral exhortation. It suits readers interested in fraternal orders and American religion. Its earnest tone reflects its time and purpose.
14172-willis-the-pilot-a-sequel-to-the-s:
Published in Boston in 1875, Willis the Pilot continues the Swiss Family Robinson story with an emigrant family wrecked on an unknown Pacific coast. Tales, travel incidents, and natural history fill the narrative, as Willis the pilot guides Fritz, Jack, and their kin through island life. A preface notes the older book's popularity among young readers hungry for settlement tales.

Beasts, boats, and old learning share the pages. From a pinnace stern, Jack and Fritz watch for wild animals while dogs wag tails and Willis smokes his Maryland pipe, an eye of fire opening and shutting. Fritz lectures on sails, crediting Isis with fastening her veil to a shaft while seeking Osiris, then praising Phoenicians who sailed round Africa without a compass. Adventure and instruction blend, as a sequel should, for boys dreaming of distant shores.
14645-unleavened-bread:
Robert Grant's 1900 novel follows Selma White, a young woman of Boston society, through emancipation, struggle, and success in three books. Scribner published the novel in New York.

Selma leaves a wedding as a guest and rides home by moonlight. She enters a world of sets and sacred houses, where the Morton-Prices are treated almost as gods and families rise by doing something well and making money. Grant satirizes society's worship of wealth and pedigree. The novel is a thoughtful study of a woman seeking a life beyond unleavened convention.
14658-the-road:
Jack London's The Road, published by Macmillan in New York in 1907 and dedicated to Josiah Flynt, is a memoir of tramping in America. London calls Flynt the real thing, blowed in the glass, and quotes a tramp-royal sestina as epigraph.

Chapters cover confession, holding her down, pictures, being pinched, the pen, hoboes that pass in the night, road-kids and gay-cats, two thousand stiffs, and bulls. London tells of lying for hours to a Nevada woman, then being halted by a fly-cop, marched to the city jail, and searched. The book is vivid, boastful, and sympathetic to men living outside the law.
14673-the-copyright-question-a-letter-to:
George N. Morang's 1902 letter to the Toronto Board of Trade argues a narrow but sharp point of Canadian law. At issue is the 1895 proposal by Hall Caine, which would make Canadian copyright depend on a book being printed and bound in Canada, and kept so printed.

Morang weighs that demand against trade, publishing practice and the American position, recalling Lord Salisbury's 1891 letter on American copyright. He asks what protection authors would gain, what printers and readers would lose, and whether a home-printing rule would help Canadian letters or merely fence them in. The letter is a crisp period brief on authors, markets and national policy.
15670-the-secret-chamber-at-chad:
Everett Evelyn-Green wrote this historical story of the secret chamber at Chad, in ten chapters from a mysterious visitor to peril and safety. The great house at Chad sleeps under a June moon, its gray masonry, castellated turrets, and twisted chimneys standing out against a pine wood. A white, still courtyard lies lined by a dark rim of shadow.

Chad was once larger: one of its two quadrangles fell in ruins during the Wars of the Roses and was never rebuilt. The old inner quadrangle still stands, ample for the Chadgrove family, while terraces and garden walks cover the outer ground. Chapters follow the household, Brother Emmanuel, a travelling preacher, a warning, and a watch. A search and a flight from peril to safety close the tale. The book is a Tudor-flavored adventure of hidden priests and loyal houses.
15767-the-texan-scouts-a-story-of-the-al:
A Texas adventure novel by Joseph A. Altsheler, issued by Appleton-Century-Crofts in New York in 1913. The book continues Ned Fulton and his friends from The Texan Star, while standing complete in itself. Altsheler, a prolific writer for boys, treats the Texas Revolution with care for fact and fire for action. The Alamo and Goliad give the tale its tragic spine.

Ned and his comrades scout, ride, and fight through a rising war for liberty. Sieges, retreats, and last stands test their loyalty to Texas and to each other. Altsheler keeps the history clear amid the adventure. The novel works as stirring history for young readers: brave lads, a just cause, and battles that still stir American memory.
16566-aunt-jane-s-nieces-abroad:
Edith Van Dyne sends her three nieces abroad in this 1906 girls' book, second in the Aunt Jane's Nieces series. The publisher promises real, vital stories of three real girls who do things, without sensationalism, each complete in itself. Brothers and older folk, the blurb adds, will enjoy the tales too.

The nieces' travels give the book its shape: new places, new people, and scrapes handled with pluck and good humor. Van Dyne writes briskly for girls, with friendship at the center. Readers of the series will find the same fresh spirit that made the first volume a hit.
16683-secret-bread:
F. Tennyson Jesse's 1917 novel follows a Cornish farming family through three books: Sowing, Growth, and Ripening. Early chapters bring high adventures in a farmyard, the mill, the kitchen, and seed-time. Later books trace first furrows, hidden springs, blown husks, and the cliff and the valley, toward an immortal moment.

Jesse writes of land, bread, and family fate with a poet's eye for Cornwall. The title's secret bread hints at hidden sustenance through hard years. Readers of regional sagas will find a rich, earthy novel of farming life across generations.
17667-dialogues-of-the-dead:
George, Lord Lyttelton, wrote these dialogues of the dead, published in 1889 by Cassell and Company in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne. Lyttelton was born in 1709 at Hagley in Worcestershire, educated at Eton and Christchurch, Oxford, and entered Parliament. He became a Lord of the Treasury and Chancellor of the Exchequer, then withdrew from politics in 1757.

Raised to the peerage, he spent his last eighteen years in lettered ease, and first published these dialogues in 1760. Readers get imaginary conversations between the dead, in the polite, moral manner of the eighteenth century. The book suits readers of Lyttelton and of the dialogue form.
18327-the-cockaynes-in-paris-or-gone-abr:
Blanchard Jerrold wrote this comic account of an English family abroad, with sketches by Gustave Dore. The Cockaynes carry guide-books and opera-glasses through Paris at its brightest, when the English quarter was crowded and the Emperor was at St. Cloud. Jerrold's preface notes that ruin later fell where they had fallen into raptures at every footstep.

Chapters follow Mrs. Rowe, the Cockayne family, a grande occasion, foolish countrywomen, and letters from Miss Carrie Cockayne. A narrator with two hats in Paris and two in London threads the tales together. Readers get the English abroad as the French saw them: eager, loud, and fond of home comforts, in a Paris that vanished with the Second Empire.
1847-songs-merry-and-sad:
John Charles McNeill, the North Carolina poet who lived from 1874 to 1907, gathers his lyrics in Songs, Merry and Sad, dedicated to Joseph P. Caldwell, the Old Man. The contents run from The Bride and Isabel to Away Down Home and Vale, with poems of love, loss, and the Carolina countryside.

McNeill's verse is musical and plain-spoken, with autumn nights, droning insects, and hungry lambs in distant pastures giving his poems their weather. The collection shows a regional poet at his best, writing about home with affection rather than nostalgia, and it remains a favorite among readers of Southern verse.
18778-garthowen-a-story-of-a-welsh-homes:
Allen Raine wrote this Welsh homestead novel, published at London by Hutchinson and Company in its sixty-fifth thousand printing. It opens on a July day in a South Wales seaport, in the hot kitchen of No. 2 Bryn Street, where Mrs. Parry chats with her lodger Gethin Owens, a dark, tattooed sailor of twenty-three just home from foreign seas. Her harsh voice softens as she says how she will miss him.

Later chapters bring Garthowen itself, Morva of the moor, an old Bible, a sea maiden, Gethin's presents, a broom girl, Sara's vision, and a dance on the cliffs. Love, kin, and chapel life shape the tale. Raine writes with warmth for Welsh home life and seaside folk.
19379-the-leicestershires-beyond-baghdad:
Edward J. Thompson wrote this war book on the Leicestershires beyond Baghdad, in the Mesopotamian campaign of the First World War. It follows a British regiment past Baghdad toward Beled Station, through old canal country, earth walls, and broken plains. The tone is that of an officer who served and watched.

Machine gunners and Lancers guard a flank while Leicestershires advance, rifle fire opens on the left, and shrapnel bursts ahead as cavalry reconnoitres. A Plymouth Brother gardener finds joy in morning flowers amid war. Readers get a vivid regimental history of desert war, faith, and endurance.
20095-journeys-to-bagdad:
Charles S. Brooks published Journeys to Bagdad in 1915, a book of travel essays with a light touch. Bagdad here stands for the far-off places a clerk dreams of from his desk. Brooks counts himself among those stirred by the smell of hemp and tar. That smell, found near a river ship chandlery, sets him dreaming.

His journeys mix real trips with daydreams of ships and strange towns. Humor keeps the longing sweet rather than sad or bitter. Readers get essays for anyone who has craved escape from routine. Brooks shows how a smell or street can launch the mind abroad.
20807-better-dead:
Clarrie rises to leave as her name is called in Better Dead, a tale from 1896. Love shines in her eyes, yet Andrew holds back from opening the door. He is a Scotch graduate, and besides, she might one day be his wife.

That dry, wry tone marks J. M. Barrie's early comic work. Barrie wrote Better Dead as a young man's skit on university and love. Its jokes turn on pride, shyness, and Scots student life. The slight tale hints at the warmth and whimsy that later made Peter Pan beloved, though here the mood stays light and gently mocking throughout.
21769-songs-of-the-road:
Arthur Conan Doyle steps away from Sherlock Holmes in this 1911 book of his own poems, gathered under the title Songs of the Road. The verses fall into three groups: narrative poems and songs, thoughtful verses, and a mixed final bunch. The opening Hymn of Empire, written for the coronation year, blesses England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland in turn. It reaches as far as Australia and the Maori land.

Other poems take up Arab steeds, empire builders, outcasts, and the faith of an aging man. Doyle's verse is plain, hearty, and built for the open air. Readers who know only the detective stories will find a different Doyle here: a patriot poet singing the road, the sea, and the wide empire.
22382-the-iliad:
The Iliad, Homer's epic of the Trojan War, appears here with explanatory notes. The notes open by summing up the quarrel that drives the poem. Agamemnon must restore the daughter of Chryses, whom he seized.

In revenge, Agamemnon takes Briseis from Achilles instead. Achilles gives her up but refuses to fight for the Greeks. At his request, his mother Thetis petitions Zeus for honor. Zeus grants it, despite Juno's opposition, at Greek expense. That grudge shapes ten years of war in one act. Readers get the classic text with help at hand. The notes guide newcomers through names, gods, and grievances.
22579-bread-overhead:
Bread Overhead is a science fiction story about a future of giant automated bakeries. The catalog record names no author or year. Its comic machinery includes huge serpent-shaped ovens that turn out loaves sealed in clear plastic, each stamped with the Puffyloaf brand mark of two cherubs circling a floating loaf.

Pickup machines gather the loaves at the oven's rear platform, snatching at them like hungry piglets with clean metal claws. The tone is playful satire aimed at mass production and brand worship. Short and brisk, the story suits readers who enjoy mid-century guesses about automation. It also shows how science fiction of that era turned everyday goods into symbols of a push-button future.
22598-the-story-of-the-first-trans-conti:
W. F. Bailey wrote The Story of the First Trans-Continental Railroad, published in 1906. Bailey recounts how the dream of a rail line from the Midwest to the Pacific grew from memorials in Congress into iron fact. The catalog of government publications alone, he notes, lists a great many reports on Pacific railroads.

The sample reaches back to a memorial by Hartwell Carver urging a rail link from Lake Michigan to the Pacific Coast. From such proposals came the Union Pacific and the golden spike era. Bailey writes as a booster-historian, close to the companies and proud of the achievement. His book preserves the promoters' own view of the road that bound a continent together.
2283-the-lost-road:
Richard Harding Davis gathers stories of adventure and war reporting in The Lost Road, a volume spanning soldiers, scouts, and wanderers. The title story leads a set that moves from the tropics to France, with Davis's crisp journalism shaping every scene. His heroes are brave, his villains plain, and his action never stalls.

An introduction by John T. McCutcheon recalls Davis in Vera Cruz, Brussels, and Salonika, adding a memoir flavor to the book. The collection captures the dashing reporter-novelist at his peak. Readers of old-fashioned adventure will find it brisk and colorful.
23460-abroad:
Thomas Crane and Ellen E. Houghton made this picture book tour, printed by Marcus Ward of London and Belfast, as a follow up to an At Home volume. Bon voyage verses invite friends to roam abroad in fancy, crossing the Channel smooth and bright without leaving the fireside.

A widowed father takes his children, Nellie, Dennis, Mabel, Rose, and little Bertie, with their kind teacher Miss Earle, on an Easter trip to Paris and through Normandy. Packing, departure, Folkestone, the Channel crossing, markets, the Luxembourg Gardens, a merry go round, and the night journey to Calais fill the pages in verse and picture. Children will love the tour, and grown readers will enjoy its gentle, old fashioned view of family travel.
2392-further-adventures-of-lad:
Albert Payson Terhune returns to his beloved collie Lad in Further Adventures of Lad, a set of stories about the dog's courage, loyalty, and cleverness at Sunnybank. Lad defends his home, rescues children, and outwits thieves, with Terhune's warm narration treating the dog as a full character. The stories blend fact and fiction about a real dog.

Terhune's collie books made him famous and shaped generations of dog lovers. The tales are sentimental but sincere, and Lad's heroics never feel forced. Dog lovers will find a classic to share. Terhune's Sunnybank kennels still exist today as a public park in New Jersey.
23986-cast-away-in-the-cold-an-old-man-s:
Dr. Isaac I. Hayes, author of An Arctic Boat Journey and The Open Polar Sea, published Cast Away in the Cold in Boston in 1868. It is an old man's story of a young man's adventures, as related by Captain John Hardy, mariner, and entered by Ticknor and Fields under the copyright act.

The frame is simple and charming: an ancient mariner meets three little people and promises them a little story. Captain Hardy, otherwise the old man, proves a man of his word. He tells how the young man went to sea, went into the cold, and was cast away there, rescuing a shipmate among other matters the chapter titles refuse to spoil. It is an Arctic adventure told as a fireside tale.
24194-no-compromise-with-slavery-an-addr:
William Lloyd Garrison gave this address in the Broadway Tabernacle, New York, on February 14, 1854, published by the American Anti-Slavery Society that same year. After a quarter century of earnest espousal of the anti-slavery cause, Garrison spoke plainly. He told his hearers he would make a clean breast of all that lay in his heart about slavery, its supporters, and its apologists.

He owned the name Garrisonian Abolitionist, the most unpopular label a man could bear in that day, yet one he believed the wise and good would one day honor. He claimed no leadership and sought no fame, only to be lost in the throng of liberty's adherents. Readers get a plain, fiery statement of uncompromising abolitionism.
25489-peck-s-bad-boy-abroad:
George W. Peck sends his Bad Boy and his Pa overseas in this 1904 comic travel book, a sequel to the boy's home-town pranks. Father and son cross to Washington first, call on President Roosevelt, and visit Mount Vernon, then carry their jokes through foreign lands, crowned heads, and strange customs.

Chapter headings promise the same formula abroad: the boy labels his father's luggage, stirs up trouble in new places, and finds fun wherever the pair land. Peck keeps the tone light, using each stop to contrast American plain speech with Old World ceremony.
25938-nancy-mcveigh-of-the-monk-road:
R. Henry Mainer tells stories of Nancy McVeigh, a good old woman of the Monk Road, printed at Toronto in 1908. The book is dedicated to a friend who sat by the author and offered happy suggestions. In verse it paints Nancy as deep lined, gray eyed, and wintry haired, quick to forget herself in others' trials and to meet rebuffs with sweet smiles. Chapters take in the woman of the inn, Miss Piper's antagonism, John Keene's schooling, and a wreck at the junction.

Later tales give Nancy's philosophy, the strength of ten, a deserter from the road, Kerry dancers, and the homecoming of Cornelius McVeigh. In one scene Nancy doubts a suitor for Florence, but Florence takes her hands and says the man will free her from sisters who burden her life. Mainer writes Irish Canadian folk with warmth, humor, and a keen ear for speech.
26030-the-automobilist-abroad:
Francis Miltoun tours Europe by motor car in The Automobilist Abroad, printed by Page in 1907 with pictures by Blanche McManus. Part one gives general advice, the grand tour, roads and routes, hotels, and travel talk. Part two tours France, from Paris to Bordeaux, the Pyrenees, Languedoc, Provence, the Rhône and Saône, and the Seine and Oise by motor boat. Part three takes Britain's roads, from the Bath road and south coast to Land's End and John o' Groat's.

A river cruise in a French boat, aptly named, runs a dozen miles an hour all day on modest power, with provisions, gasoline, charts, and wraps stowed in eight metres of hull. Appendices list road races, hill climbs, and the motor industry in France. Miltoun writes for early motorists keen on roads, inns, and the grand tour by car.
26282-the-witch-of-salem-or-credulity-ru:
John R. Musick's Witch of Salem, volume seven of his Columbian Historical Novels, covers twenty years of colonial history from 1680 to 1700. Its preface defends the novelist's task of entering past minds, and it dresses speech in the dialect of the age. The book aims to show common people as well as rulers, with the Salem witch panic at its heart.

Mid-book scenes show a harder frontier life: mothers guarding babes from murderers and kidnappers, cattle driven among dwellings at night, and Sabbath patrols watching while citizens worship. The novel pairs the witch trials with daily danger, and its subtitle, Credulity Run Mad, states its moral: fear, once loose, harms the innocent first.
26831-marsk-stig-a-ballad:
George Borrow wrote this ballad, printed in London for private circulation in 1913. In four parts it tells of Marsk Stig Andersen. The young King Erik sends him to war while promising to guard his lady as if she were his own sister. Stig dreams that his noble horse chases a wild mare and tramples his lifeless clay, but he rides out all the same, leaving fair Ingeborg alone in her castle. Erik soon saddles his steed to visit her.

Ingeborg refuses every bribe, from a gold-worked shirt to rings of red gold, answering that rather than betray Stig she would gladly lose her life. When Stig returns, he strides into the Ting of the land and makes his plaint before the assembled crowd: a rape upon his wife has been done. The ballad breaks off with honest men clenching their fists at the tale of horror.
27406-axel-thordson-and-fair-valborg-a-b:
George Borrow wrote this ballad, printed for private circulation in London in 1913, in a text transcribed from a Thomas J. Wise pamphlet. It opens at a wide board where two ladies, Dame Julli and Queen Malfred, play at tables, while a child nearby toys with a pear and an apple.

Into the hall stalks Sir Axel Thordson, bound for Rome's imperial towers, who loves the child in secrecy. He pats her cheek with tears, wishing she were of fitting years to be mated with him. Sister and mother answer in turn that even so the match could not be. Borrow's ballad tells a doomed love in plain, old-fashioned verse.
27786-the-rough-road:
William J. Locke's 1918 novel tells the story of Doggie Trevor, whose real name is James Marmaduke, a sheltered young man raised like a toy Pomeranian by an elderly, doting mother. When she dies, the comfortable twenty-five-year-old finds himself facing the Great War.

Locke follows Doggie through the war without medals or heroic glory, showing how an unlikely man endures and grows. Dedicated to Sheila as a little tale of the war remembered in after years, the novel is a gentle study of courage in ordinary people. Locke stresses that Doggie won no cross and no distinction whatever, yet went through with it and lived to tell the tale.
28245-prisoners-of-poverty-abroad:
Helen Campbell wrote Prisoners of Poverty Abroad in Boston in 1889, after fifteen months watching women workers abroad. Campbell, author of Prisoners of Poverty on New York, studies trades open to women in other lands. She stresses figures less than her first book did, and more the ethical side of low pay and long hours. She dedicates the book to a friend in whom justice and truth are instincts.

Campbell argues that organization helps women think and act together for better work. Her pages give a side-light on the labour question, as women themselves saw it. The book remains a valuable record of women's work in the late nineteenth century.
29237-an-essay-on-satire-particularly-on:
Walter Harte wrote this essay on satire in 1730, with Alexander Pope's Dunciad as its chief example. This Augustan Reprint Society volume, number 132, reprints Harte's text with an introduction by Thomas Gilmore, published by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library in 1968.

Harte examines what satire does and how Pope's mock-epic about dullness works as satire. The Dunciad crowns a king of dunces and parades bad writers through heroic verse. Harte's essay helps readers see the rules behind the joke. Readers get an eighteenth-century critic's guide to satire, useful for anyone reading Pope or studying how mockery became an art form.
29357-our-young-folks-at-home-and-abroad:
Edited by Daphne Dale and printed in 1894 by W. B. Conkey Company, this large gift book gathers short tales and poems for young people from many hands, among them Annie D. Bell, Clara J. Denton, Amanda M. Douglas, and Oliver Optic. Short pieces sit beside pictures made for the book, so each page turns to a fresh scene or voice.

Cats find new homes, children learn small lessons, and home scenes mix with travel sketches in a form meant for family reading aloud. The range is wide on purpose: light verse, plain tales, and moral turns, none of them long. Modern readers get a clear view of what late Victorian editors thought fit and fine for the young.
2948-where-angels-fear-to-tread:
E. M. Forster's first novel, Where Angels Fear to Tread, begins at Charing Cross, where the Herriton family sees Lilia off to Italy. Philip, Harriet, Irma, and Mrs. Herriton gather with Mrs. Theobald and Mr. Kingcroft, while Miss Abbott arrives with her own relatives. Lilia laughs at the crowd, calls it an ovation, and demands foot-warmers for her first-class carriage.

In Italy Lilia marries rashly, and the Herritons' attempts to rescue her, and later her child, expose English snobbery against Italian feeling. A wife crying while she writes a short letter begging to be saved gives the novel its emotional center. Forster's comedy of manners turns tragic, and the book still reads as a fresh attack on respectability.
29822-rescue-squad:
Thomas J. O'Hara wrote Rescue Squad for Fantastic Universe, after winning honorable mention in a prize story contest run by the Fantasy Writers' Workshop at the College of the City of New York. The editors call it a documentary-type science fiction yarn, joining realistic character work with the mystery, suspense, and terror of near-future space travel and a lone pilot's fight to survive.

A million miles from where she should be, the mail ship MR4 tumbles wildly through space. Twenty million miles below burns the hungry, flaming maw of the sun. Atomic refrigeration units run at full blast, yet heat climbs slowly inside and out, and the atomic engines have long been silenced. Hal Burnett twists on a narrow bunk, strapped against non-gravity, while disaster closes in. The tale is taut, grim, and human.
30031-the-eye-of-dread:
Payne Erskine, author of The Mountain Girl, published The Eye of Dread in New York in 1913, with A. L. Burt Company, by arrangement with Little, Brown and Company. George Gibbs drew the frontispiece, with the words Listen, go with the love in your heart, for me, from page 329. Three books make up the novel, with thirty-six chapters and more.

Book one follows Betty, bees, a mother's struggle, leave-taking, the passing of time, and the end of the war. A new era begins, with Mary Ballard's discovery, a banker's view, a nutting party, and Betty Ballard's awakening. Book two leaves the desert for a big man's return, a mine, a violin, and a beast on the trail. Book three brings a schoolteacher, a Swede's telegram, an arrest, an argument, a prisoner, and a trial, with Nels Nelson's testimony.
30308-hanging-by-a-thread:
David Gordon sets a space tale aboard the interplanetary cargo vessel Persephone, from Analog, August 1961, with pictures by Douglas. Jayjay Kelvin sits in a cozily small lounge, feet on a low table, reading a small book with total attention. The Persephone was not built as a passenger vessel, and its two passengers travel as an accommodation, not as a money-making proposition, since no regular passenger runs serve Pluto.

Across the table, Jeffry Hull works industriously with pencil and paper, while Kelvin keeps his nose in his book from genuine interest, not from slighting his companion. The tagline promises the core tension: seldom does a shipful of men literally hang by a thread, and seldom does a device, every part thoroughly tested, refuse to work. Gordon builds suspense from that tested device and its failure.
3059-the-iliad:
Homer's Iliad appears here in English prose by Andrew Lang, Walter Leaf, and Ernest Myers, in the revised Macmillan edition of 1911. Lang of Merton College, Leaf of Trinity College, and Myers of Wadham College divided the translation, as the prefatory note explains, giving the epic a clear, readable prose form. All twenty-four books run from the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon to the burial of Hector.

A night scene compares Trojan watchfires to stars on a windless night, when peaks, headlands, and glades stand clear and a shepherd's heart is glad. A thousand fires burn on the plain, fifty men by each in blazing gleam. The translation remains a respected prose Iliad, faithful to Homer's story while letting English readers follow the war without verse.
30852-the-tin-woodman-of-oz-a-faithful-s:
L. Frank Baum, Royal Historian of Oz, wrote this 1918 Oz book with pictures by John R. Neill. It answers a question readers kept asking. The puzzle at its heart concerns Nick Chopper's fiancée, a pretty Munchkin girl whose wedding never happened once the Wicked Witch cursed his axe and left him swapping flesh for tin. Baum says he too had wondered, until Woot the Wanderer took up the matter.

The Tin Woodman sets out with Woot, the Scarecrow, and Polychrome, the Rainbow's Daughter, on an astonishing adventure to find her. Baum dedicates the book to Frank Alden Baum, the son of his son, and he writes for young and old alike, as his note to readers makes plain. It is a warm, funny fairy tale about love lost, loyalty, and a tin man's search for a heart's old promise.
31577-the-mighty-dead:
William Campbell Gault's short story The Mighty Dead, as its headnote frames it, asks what life would be like in a world which has conquered the near planets but abolished all literature. In that not too distant future, the headnote says, all the pressure groups have united to rule the roost. Doak Parker, the hero, weighs his career in Washington against a highly suspect country girl he has just met. Her name is June. A two months' campaign may end in conquest this very weekend.

The story opens as Doak, thinking of June, sees a light flash and hears a buzzer. Ryder appears on his small desk-screen with a little job for the weekend. Gault's tale is a science-fiction satire, where a world without books still runs on politics and desire. Readers will find a sharp, compact story about literature's enemies and its quiet defenders.
316-the-golden-road:
L. M. Montgomery follows the Story Girl and her Prince Edward Island friends down the golden road of childhood, a highway through the land of lost delight. The book is dedicated to Aunt Mary Lawson, who told many of the tales retold here. Montgomery wrote The Golden Road in 1913, as a sequel to The Story Girl.

Shadow and sunshine mingle as the children tell stories, dream, and watch the years wait beyond. Montgomery writes with warmth and nostalgia, and the novel pairs with The Story Girl as a portrait of a vanished youth. The Story Girl herself, a gifted teller of tales, gives the book its centre and its charm.
3176-the-innocents-abroad:
Mark Twain's 1869 travel book follows a party of American innocents abroad on a grand excursion. Popular talk of the trip, its programme, and its tickets open the account, with the defection of the celebrities who had promised to come. Grand preparations, an imposing dignitary, and the European exodus follow, until the clans assemble and the ship is at sea at last.

From stateroom number ten the pilgrims proceed to average their fellow passengers, endure tribulation among the patriarchs, and seek amusement under difficulties. Twain's humor works by collision: American expectation against European fact, at every port. The book made his name, and it remains the funniest first tour of Europe in American letters.
32185-lord-stranleigh-abroad:
Robert Barr's Lord Stranleigh Abroad was published by Ward, Locke and Company in London, Melbourne, and Toronto in 1913. It follows the lord hero of Young Lord Stranleigh and Lord Stranleigh, Philanthropist. Its frontispiece shows a confrontation: Why did you wish to murder me? Its seven chapters run from Lord Stranleigh All at Sea and An Automobile Ride through The God in the Car and The Mad Miss Maturin. They continue to In Search of Game, The Bunk House Prisoner, and The End of the Contest.

Readers get an Edwardian adventure novel, where a wealthy English lord abroad meets automobiles, a mad young woman, a bunk-house prisoner, and a murder attempt. The tone is light and roving, with cars, game, and contests standing in for the drawing room. Stranleigh's travels supply the plot, and the contest at the end settles the score.
32241-dickens-stories-about-children-eve:
Dickens' Stories About Children, Every Child Can Read, edited by the Reverend Jesse Lyman Hurlbut, was published in Philadelphia by the John C. Winston Company in 1909. Illustrated, in Every Child's Library, it carries a portrait of Charles Dickens as frontispiece. Hurlbut addresses his preface to the young reader. He presents Dickens as among the greatest Victorian story-writers, of the mid-to-late nineteenth century, under Queen Victoria.

Perhaps, Hurlbut writes, Dickens was the greatest of them all for now, a generation later. Readers get Dickens for children, selected and edited for young readers, with the novelist's children at the centre. The volume serves as an introduction to Dickens, where the Victorian master meets the nursery shelf, in stories chosen for every child to read.
32273-stories-of-our-naval-heroes-every-:
Stories of Our Naval Heroes, Every Child Can Read, edited by the Reverend Jesse Lyman Hurlbut, was published in Philadelphia by the John C. Winston Company in 1908. It begins with the first sea fight of the Revolution, the burning of the Gaspee in Narragansett Bay. A British schooner captured by farmers follows, with Captain Jerry O'Brien leading the patriots of 1775. Benedict Arnold follows with a novel fight on Lake Champlain.

Paul Jones, the greatest of America's naval heroes, fights the first great fight of the American Navy. Bushnell scares the British with the pioneer torpedo boat and the Battle of the Kegs. Barry and his rowboats win a victory over the British, Tucker is honored by Washington as the hero of Marblehead, and Barney in the Hyder Ali captures the General Monk. Moorish pirates and young Decatur follow. Readers get American naval heroes told for children.
32289-an-american-girl-abroad:
Adeline Trafton's travel book, entered for copyright in 1872, records a young American woman's first trip abroad after leaving school. Written as a record of pleasant days, the book is dedicated to her father, the Reverend Mark Trafton. It follows her party by steamer and on land, noting fellow passengers, places of worship, and small daily incidents.

An early scene finds the party joining steerage passengers for worship deep inside the ship at night. The tone is bright and chatty, with close attention to people met along the way and to the sights that surprise a first-time traveller. Rather than a formal guide, the book reads as a personal account of seeing new cities, customs, and crowds through young, American eyes. Illustrations by Miss L. B. Humphrey accompany the text.
32402-the-story-of-our-country-every-chi:
Jesse Lyman Hurlbut's Story of Our Country, subtitled Every Child Can Read, presents American history for young readers in plain, illustrated chapters. An opening plate shows a steam shovel at work in the Culebra Cut of the Panama Canal, pointing to the book's interest in modern American enterprise as well as older history. Hurlbut, a clergyman and popular writer for children, aimed to make the nation's story clear, stirring, and easy to follow.

The volume moves through discovery, settlement, revolution, and growth, with pictures and short chapters suited to school and home reading. Its title promise is simplicity without condescension: events, heroes, and turning points told in language a child can grasp. Families and teachers looking for an early twentieth-century American history for young readers will find it direct and readable.
32410-no-shield-from-the-dead:
Gordon R. Dickson's tale, printed in IF Worlds of Science Fiction in January 1953, follows Terri Mac, a comptroller who sees through a staged party at once. Guests set down cocktail glasses and file out at the word of an old man in his late fifties, propped on pillows in a corner chair. Even the blonde who brought Terri from an embassy ball leaves in a far less drunken manner than she showed earlier.

Terri's shield, the tale's framing note insists, could not be pierced by any conceivable force, yet he was defenceless. Dickson builds tension from that paradox, as a man protected against every physical threat faces a danger no shield can stop. The story turns on power, persuasion, and the dead, whose claims reach past every guard a living man can raise.
32470-isle-of-the-undead:
Lloyd Arthur Eshbach's tale, printed in Weird Tales in October 1936, tells what befell a yachting party on an island of living dead men. Its first chapter, A Horror from the Past, opens under a drab grey sheet of cloud slipping from the moon like a shroud from a long-dead face. Yellow light falls on a calm, oily sea and a narrow bank of fog, setting a cold, phosphorescent scene.

An illustration shows a rock-like fist making a bloody ruin of a thin man's mouth, promising the violence to come. Eshbach builds horror from sea, fog, and moonlight before the island's dead rise to claim the living. Readers who enjoy pulp weird fiction will find a gripping, uncanny tale of a pleasure cruise turned into a fight for survival.
32514-pledged-to-the-dead:
Seabury Quinn's tale, printed in Weird Tales in October 1937, brings back Jules de Grandin, the little French detective. It tells of a lover pledged to a sweetheart dead for more than a century. It opens at autumn dusk, as de Grandin and his friend Doctor Trowbridge sip coffee and kaiserschmarrn in the study after their meal. De Grandin, homesick for Saint Cloud and the Ile de France, praises pastry cooks' booths, crisp Napoléons, éclairs, and cherry cream-puffs.

A shrilling doorbell breaks the talk, as a woman demands Doctor Trowbridge at once, leaning on the button while Nora McGinnis, the household factotum, answers with reluctance. From that domestic opening, Quinn builds a ghostly romance in which a striking death menaces a man bound by an old pledge. The tale mixes French charm, New England setting, and weird horror in de Grandin's familiar manner.
32830-the-state-of-the-blessed-dead:
Henry Alford, Dean of Canterbury, gathers discourses on the state of the blessed dead, delivered in Canterbury Cathedral during Advent 1868 and published by Hodder and Stoughton in 1869. He writes for edification and personal comfort, from what Scripture has revealed.

Two texts anchor the book. Our Lord tells the dying thief, in Luke chapter twenty-three, that today he shall be with him in Paradise. St. Paul writes, in Philippians chapter one, of departing to be with Christ. Alford argues that the departed spirit is with Christ at once, which disproves a sleep of unconsciousness until resurrection. Later discourses weigh the delayed coming of the Lord and the employ of mankind in glory.
33134-sigurd-our-golden-collie-and-other:
Katharine Lee Bates's Sigurd, Our Golden Collie, and Other Comrades of the Road gathers sketches and poems about dogs and the road. It was published in New York in 1919 with a second printing in March 1920. The volume opens with Sigurd's puppyhood, and several pieces had appeared in magazines. An illustration shows the joy of life and Sigurd together.

Bates, known for America the Beautiful, writes of collies and other animal comrades with warmth, humor, and a poet's eye for character. The sketches follow dogs through puppyhood, loyalty, and loss, while the poems give their feelings a voice. The book suits animal lovers and readers of gentle nature writing. It preserves a time when a dog's life was told as a small biography, full of affection and respect.
33144-the-oriental-rug-a-monograph-on-ea:
W. D. Ellwanger's Oriental Rug is a monograph on eastern rugs and carpets, saddle-bags, mats, and pillows. It guides collectors through kinds and classes, types, borders, figures, dyes, and symbols, with practical advice. It was published in New York in 1909 with a copyright of 1903. Its first plate shows an antique Ladik prayer rug from the collection of George H. Ellwanger. Its chapters move from the mystery of the rug and general classification to making, designs, dyeing, and Persian, Caucasian, Turkish, and Turkoman varieties.

Ellwanger, author of A Summer Snowflake, writes for buyers who wanted to judge a rug by more than price, teaching them to read knots, colors, and patterns. The book's plates and careful divisions make it a standard early guide. For collectors and historians of decorative art, it remains a useful introduction to a craft where region, religion, and trade all left marks in wool.
33636-stand-up-ye-dead:
Norman Maclean confronts a quiet national disaster in this 1916 volume: the falling birthrate and the empty cradle. Maclean argues that the greatest disaster of the day has befallen in city streets at home, gradually and surreptitiously, so that people do not know they are overwhelmed. London's birthrate fell in Hampstead from 30 to 17. 55, and in Edinburgh from 34 children per thousand in 1871 to 17 in 1915. Many places already have more coffins than cradles.

Eight chapters move from the empty cradle and the roots of the evil through the empty countryside, the man in the slum, the lord of the slum, the great refusal. Maclean writes as a preacher and social critic, urging readers to face a slow calamity with the horror they would feel if half a city's children were slain in a night.
34770-told-by-the-death-s-head:
Maurus Jokai wrote this romantic tale, Told by the Death's Head, in a rendering by Boggs printed at Chicago, Akron, and New York in 1908. Boggs also rendered Jokai's Nameless Castle. A preface tells how the tale began: the author found, in an old book of Rhine lore, a skull that hangs in a metal casket in the foundry of Ehrenbreitstein fortress.

That skull, the lore says, confessed to twenty-one mortal sins, the seven deadly ones trebled, and yet was doomed not for them but for breaking a rule of war. What if it could speak, Jokai asks, and defend itself from the Weichsel to the Ganges? Contents follow its life: a fire-pot, a trial, robbers' caves, a monastery, the Templars, a ship, and Bengal.
35509-the-golden-road:
The Golden Road is a novel by Frank Waller Allen. Wessels and Bissell published it in New York in 1910. Hood supplied illustrations and decorations. A Borrow epigraph praises night, day, and the wind on the heath. Twenty-five chapters follow a travelling pedler.

The happy pedler comes to town in chapter one. His name is Jean Francois. A piece of jade and an inquisition follow. Nance, first a nonentity, becomes illustrious. A kindly priest, the Abbe Picot, shares the road. Chapters mark a day of faith, a day of doubt, and a day of lost confidence. The frontispiece shows a farewell kiss thrown from finger-tips. Picardy and its beloved roads haunt the hero's dreams.
35680-one-year-abroad:
The author of One Summer spent a year in Europe and sent home these letters, published by Osgood at Boston in 1878. Hamburg at a first glance opens the book. Heidelberg in winter, a flying sheet from Paris, and Baden-Baden follow. Stuttgart gets rambles, and the Black Forest a day. Nuremberg the ancient, Lindau and Bregenz, and the Vorarlberg carry the journey toward the Alps.

The Tyrol and Innsbruck come next, then Hohenschwangau and Neuschwanstein, the mad king's castles still new. Life in Schattwald, the Engadine, Ragatz, and a flying trip to the Rhine Falls fill the high summer. The book comes down by the Lake of Lucerne and up and down the Rigi. A Kaiser fest and the Cannstadt Volksfest show festival Germany. A visit among Freiligrath's books gives the literary pilgrimage its moment. The letters are a young American's Germany, observed town by town.
36009-a-book-written-by-the-spirits-of-t:
Helleberg of Cincinnati holds that the dead wrote this book with their own hands. Its title page says the words came by independent slate-writing through the medium Lizzie Green and others. He compiled and arranged the sheets, and printed them in 1883.

Contents list seances, materialized forms, and flowers passed from spirit hands. Messages claim such senders as Swedenborg, Washington, Lincoln, and Garfield. One long part tells of a wedding tour to the planet Mars. The book is a full record of American spiritualism at its boldest, set down by a true believer who took each slate as proof. A Longfellow verse on the soul stands at its front.
36177-mr-punch-on-tour-the-humour-of-tra:
Mr Punch on Tour gathers jokes on travel from the pages of Punch magazine. J A Hammerton edited the book for the Punch Library of Humour. The series drew on Punch work from eighteen hundred forty one onward. One hundred fifty three pictures fill this volume.

Artists named include Phil May, Charles Keene, and George du Maurier. The jokes mock the stiff English tourist most of all. Tour tales at home get the same sharp treatment. One cartoon sends a pair to a Romeo and Juliet room at a Shakespeare hotel. Trains, ships, inns, and strange beds all draw fire. Readers who like short jokes with strong drawings will find the tour brisk and broad.
36273-the-automobile-girls-at-newport-or:
Laura Crane wrote this Automobile Girls tale set at Newport summer resort. Altemus printed the book in Philadelphia in 1910. It joins past tales in the Berkshires and along the Hudson. Chapter one, Barbara to the Rescue, opens with pink hair ribbons.

Barbara Thurston clinks a gold coin on a sewing table top. Mollie cheers silk stockings, won by berry sales to a hotel. Grace Carter promised to fix an invitation for the girls trip. Ruth perfect plan, a glorious start, and Newport at last follow. A ball night, fortune tellers, and a tennis meet fill the Newport stay.
37038-stories-of-the-railroad:
John Hill's Stories of the Railroad was published in New York by Doubleday and McClure in 1899, under McClure copyrights of 1898 and 1899. Nine tales fill the contents, most of them told from the cab or the depot: an engineer's Christmas story, and the clean man and the dirty angels. Jim Wainwright's kid and a peg-legged romance follow. Mormon Joe the robber and the polar zone close the list.

The first story goes back to 1863. The narrator, a young fellow without a home at either end of the run, is firing an old Hinkley insider in New England for engineer James Dillon. Dillon was as good a man as the road had: careful yet fearless, kindhearted yet impulsive, loved like a father by the boy. His own father had refused to be comforted when he took to railroading, so Jim became his adviser and his home.
37429-polly-and-her-friends-abroad:
Polly and Her Friends Abroad, by Lillian Elizabeth Roy, was published in New York in 1922. Roy wrote a run of Polly books, starting with Polly of Pebbly Pit. Drawings came from the artist Barbour. Polly Brewster and her friend Eleanor Maynard sail for Europe here. Their teacher in interior decorating, Mr Fabian, escorts them, with the Ashby family.

The trip aims at museums and antique shops across Great Britain and beyond. Chapter heads promise love affairs, an elopement, and a surprise. A dangerous pass in the Alps, a plot in Venice, and an earthquake test the party. A highwayman in disguise appears near the end. The tale mixes travel sights with light peril and romance for young readers.
37536-the-house-of-the-dead:
The House of the Dead is Fedor Dostoieffsky's account of prison life in Siberia. The Everyman's Library edition came out in London in 1911 and was reprinted in 1914. Julius Bramont wrote the introduction.

The title page calls the book a tale of prison life in Siberia. Dostoieffsky drew on his own years as a convict in a hard camp. The work shows the days, the work and the men of that grim house. Thieves, killers and wronged men share its walls. The prose is grave and close, with pity for folk at the lowest depth. The Everyman set placed the book on cheap shelves for all readers.
37688-a-trooper-galahad:
A Trooper Galahad, by Captain Charles King of the United States Army, author of The Colonel's Daughter and Marion's Faith, was published by J B Lippincott Company at Philadelphia in 1899. King's other army novels, from Captain Blake to Foes in Ambush, fill the publisher's opening list.

The novel begins at a littered headquarters desk. Life is full of ups and downs, mused the colonel, as he laid down an official communication just received from Department Headquarters. The illustration shows a man felled like an ox, promising frontier violence to come.
37817-the-cries-of-london-exhibiting-sev:
The Cries of London, by John Thomas Smith, shows the street traders of London in old and new times. This volume was printed in 1839 and pairs with Smith's Vagabondiana, tales of wandering beggars. Smith had been keeper of the prints in the British Museum.

Smith engraved all the plates himself, and the editor notes that he prepared the book years before it saw print. Thirteen plates are copied from rare early prints, and the rest were sketched from life. The editor rates the life studies far above the copies. Smith also wrote the text for each plate, with revision by the late Francis Douce. The editor has touched the letter-press here and there to suit the present day. The street cries fix a lost London of hawkers and costers.
38319-by-desert-ways-to-baghdad:
By Desert Ways to Baghdad, by Louisa Jebb, Mrs Roland Wilkins, was published by Thomas Nelson and Sons at London, Edinburgh, Dublin, and New York. A sketch map of the author's route accompanies the narrative. The first part runs from Brusa to Diarbekr, opening with a prologue.

Jebb takes her epigraph from a wanderer's verse: I am a kind of parrot, and the mirror is holden to me. The route crosses Ottoman country by desert ways, as the title promises. A long publisher's list of travel and biography titles fronts this copy of the book.
38714-carry-on-a-story-of-the-fight-for-:
Carry On is a boys' war story of the fight for Bagdad by Herbert Strang. Milford published it in London in 1917. Two illustrators supplied its pictures. A colour frontispiece shows a dash for liberty. Eighteen chapters carry the Mesopotamian campaign. The tale mixes spies, disguises, and cavalry action.

Chapter titles map the adventure. A tell near Babylon opens it. A barber's apprentice and a shaved prisoner follow. A dervish and a mad race succeed. The Euphrates is crossed midway. A rearguard action and a raid fill the later pages. Raising the siege closes the campaign. The first chapter surveys the land between the rivers. Its canals lie choked with sand, Strang writes. Buried cities sleep under the mounds.
38961-narrative-of-the-surveying-voyages:
The first volume of the official narrative of the surveying voyages of the Adventure and Beagle, published by Henry Colburn at London in 1839. Captain Parker King commanded the first expedition, from 1826 to 1830, which examined the southern shores of South America. Robert Fitz-Roy, who commanded the later voyages, presents the volume to the Earl of Minto at the Admiralty, King's results united with the Beagle's.

The three-volume work covers the years 1826 to 1836, ending with the Beagle's circumnavigation of the globe. Fitz-Roy's preface says the aim was general information joined to a duty to seamen, with technical detail kept to appendices and a nautical memoir. These surveys charted the coasts of Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego for the ships that would follow.
39021-the-story-of-the-rome-watertown-an:
Edward Hungerford wrote this history, The Story of the Rome, Watertown and Ogdensburg Railroad, printed at New York in 1922 with pictures. Hungerford also wrote The Modern Railroad. He dedicates the book to the pioneers of the North Country who laboured hard and well so that their region might enjoy the blessings of the railroad.

Twelve chapters trace the line from hope to system. After an introduction come the first stirrings toward a railroad, the coming of the Watertown and Rome, and the Potsdam and Watertown line. The road is formed, prospers, and expands, then sinks into hard times. Later parts, branches, and brisk new management follow, until the New York Central arrives and the story ends.
39452-the-pilgrim-s-progress-by-john-bun:
Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress in the Every Child Can Read edition was published by the John Winston Company of Philadelphia in 1909, in the Every Child's Library. Hurlbut edited the text for young readers. A plate list shows the plan: Christian confides in his wife at the front, then Evangelist pointing to the wicket-gate, Christian before the cross, and Christian and Faithful joining company.

Part one opens with the dream. The narrator, walking through the wilderness of this world, sleeps in a den and dreams of a man in rags, a book in his hand and a great burden on his back. Reading, the man weeps and trembles, and breaks out with the cry, What shall I do. A footnote ties the den to Bedford jail, where Bunyan was twelve years a prisoner. Christian then takes his trouble home, and at last breaks his mind to his wife and children.
39778-mollie-and-the-unwiseman-abroad:
John Kendrick Bangs wrote Mollie and the Unwiseman Abroad, with illustrations in colour by Grace G Wiederseim, issued at Philadelphia and London by J B Lippincott Company in nineteen ten. Bangs gave the book to his friends the children. A foreword introduces two heroes and a heroine. Chapter one is Mollie, Whistlebinkie, and the Unwiseman. The Start stands second.

A plate shows the Unwiseman trying to find out how to tie a sinker to soup. The Holiday Editions list in front offers Macdonald Princess and the Goblin and A Dog of Flanders at a dollar fifty each. Mollie, her small brother Whistlebinkie, and the gloriously wrong headed Mr Unwiseman tour Europe in the tale. Each sight draws a foolish wise remark from the old gentleman. Children get travel fun and nonsense logic from a famed American humorist.
39950-people-of-destiny-americans-as-i-s:
Philip Gibbs, author of 'Now It Can Be Told,' published 'People of Destiny' with Harper and Brothers in 1920. Its subtitle promises Americans as he saw them at home and abroad. His first chapter, 'The Adventure of Life in New York,' recalls arriving just after the war, when the warriors were coming home in triumph. Gibbs saw the city rising through Hudson haze and sunlight striking the Woolworth Tower, with banners and golden stars of death in the streets.

Later chapters turn to people he met in America, things he likes in the United States, and America's new place in the world. Gibbs also reports what England thinks of America and how Americans appear in Europe. Illustrations include a relief from boredom after office hours and the social atmosphere of an American post-office.
40242-the-modern-railroad:
Edward Hungerford wrote The Modern Railroad, published by McClurg of Chicago in 1911. Many photographs illustrate the volume. Hungerford had written railroad tales before, among them The Man Who Stole a Railroad. He dedicates this book to his father.

The first chapters trace how the lines began. Canal owners fought the new roads and lost. Small lines merged into great systems running east to west and north to south. The Baltimore and Ohio, the Erie, and the Illinois Central all appear. Rock Island first spanned the Mississippi, Hungerford notes. Then come the works themselves. Building a road means charters, surveys, grades, and track-laying. Tunnels like the Hoosac and bridges of timber, stone, and steel close the survey.
40427-report-of-the-hoosac-tunnel-and-tr:
Report on the Hoosac Tunnel and Troy and Greenfield Railroad is a Massachusetts Senate paper of 1867. It carries the findings of the Joint Standing Committee of 1866 on the great tunnel work. Tappan Wentworth, chairman, transmits the report to the president of the Senate in Boston. The committee was charged to visit the tunnel and railroad and examine progress.

Condition, cost, and pace of the bore through the Hoosac mountain form the matter. Few American works of the age drew such sums, hope, and hard dispute. State printers Wright and Potter issued the report as Senate number fifty nine. Engineers and historians gain a primary record of a landmark tunnel fight.
40507-the-challenge-of-the-dead:
Stephen Graham wrote The Challenge of the Dead, a vision of the war and the life of the common soldier in France. He saw it two years afterwards, between August and November of 1920. Cassell and Company published the book at London in 1921. A list of Graham's travel books stands at the front. The narrative opens at Zeebrugge, on the long stone mole.

The sun shines and a strong wind throws spray across the breakwater. German guns stand at intervals along it, their barrels burst like thistle-heads. Their armoured shelters carry the ranges to every place within gunshot, in neat German script. Hydroplane sheds cling to the lee side. Sunk vessels jut from the fairway, sunk in 1918. A tablet marks where the Vindictive's landing party made its raid.
40689-off-to-sea-the-adventures-of-jovia:
Kingston sent more boys to sea in fiction than the Royal Navy took in fact, and Off to Sea tells the adventures of Jovial Jack Junker on his road to fame. Jack introduces himself as a boy known from his earliest days for good humor, who never had an hour's sickness in his life.

The chapters run the full Kingston course: birth and education, life on the Roarer, across the ocean, the flowery land of China, a cruise in a junk, a typhoon and a shipwreck. Then capture by the Celestials, liberty again, a pirate stronghold, and promotion. Kingston's formula taught seamanship and cheerfulness together, and his heroes rise, as Jack does, by keeping their temper in a gale.
4069-the-dawn-of-canadian-history-a-chro:
Stephen Leacock's chronicle of Aboriginal Canada opens before European arrival, when uncounted centuries of Native history left few written records. Very few tribes held even a primitive art of writing, though Aztecs and Toltecs of Mexico preserved rulers and great events in pictures.

Leacock sketches the peoples of the North, their ways of life, and the first meetings with explorers. The book belongs to the Chronicles of Canada series, written for general readers in plain, lively prose. Modern readers should note its dated terms and views, while valuing its clear survey of a deep past.
40759-the-old-road:
The Old Road is a travel and history book by H. Belloc, published by Constable and Company in 1911 with pictures by William Hyde. Belloc dedicated it to Philip Kershaw and Harold Baker, his companions on the journey. Its subject is the old track that ran from Winchester to Canterbury, the road later known as the Pilgrims' Way.

The first chapters argue why the road took its line and why Winchester and Canterbury became its two ends. Belloc then walks the route in stages: Winchester to Alton, Alton to Shalford, Shalford to Dorking, and on through Boxhill, Titsey, and Wrotham to Canterbury. The book mixes road craft, chalk country, and old churches along the way.
41041-the-cumberland-road:
Archer Butler Hulbert wrote the tenth volume of his Historic Highways of America series, issued at Cleveland in 1904. Its subject is the Cumberland Road, the first national road of the United States. A quote from Veech heads the book, calling the road a monument that carried thousands of people and millions of wealth into the West.

Chapters trace the building of the road in the west, its operation and control, and the stagecoaches and freighters that used it. Mails and mail lines come next, then taverns and tavern life along the way. Plates show the bridge at Big Crossings and Chestnut Ridge. Hulbert's West, as he tells it, grew up along this road.
41118-the-old-glade-forbes-s-road-pennsy:
The Old Glade Road is a past study of the great war road cut through the hills of a coal state in the age of the French war, by Hulbert. It stands as the fifth part of a run of books on the great roads of America. Maps and prints fill its form, put out in the first years of the last age.

Its rights were held that year by its house, with all rights kept. Its parts take the old trade path first, then a blood red line of forts. The fights of the great year of the road, and the ask of old road or new, fill the mid run. The new road, its life as a war road to the west, and its age as a state road close the tale.
41143-boone-s-wilderness-road:
Boone's Wilderness Road is volume six of the Historic Highways of America series, by Archer Hulbert. The Clark company published it at Cleveland in nineteen o three, with maps and pictures. Five chapters run from the first western pilgrims to the end of Boone's road. A plat of Boonesborough and Filson's map of Kentucky stand among the plates.

The first chapter tells how Virginia alone of the colonies eyed the West freely. Her charter set no western bound, while sister colonies were fenced by lines. After the fall of Quebec, the treaty gave the colonies the Mississippi River. Then the king's order of seventeen sixty three barred all grants past the river heads. Lord Hillsborough meant to check the roving temper of the Virginians thereby. Pontiac's war and Bouquet's march fill out the road's dark prelude.
41285-why-we-should-read:
Why We Should Read, by S P B Mais, came out in London in 1921. Mais had written Books and Their Writers and books for schools. A line from Landor heads the work, that he who first praises a book well ranks next to its author. Mais gives the book to his wife.

Four parts sort his picks by kind. First come English greats, Tom Jones, Wuthering Heights, Lamb, Boswell, and Pepys. Next come new voices, Santayana, Huxley, Graves, and Forster among them. A short part treats books on the English tongue. A last part treats men from abroad, Montaigne, Pushkin, Gogol, Tolstoy, and Chekov. Mais calls Tom Jones the most artful tale since Homer. Book lovers get a warm, plain guide to what to read next.
41459-the-broken-thread:
The Broken Thread is a novel by William Le Queux, in an edition dated nineteen seventeen. Ward and Lock published it in London, Melbourne, and Toronto that year. Chapter one, called Concerns a Girl in Black, opens on the Southport seafront. Two Cambridge men in their last year stroll there in warm August weather.

Raife Remington spots a fair girl in dead black leading a small pom dog. A turquoise band on her hat and a cherry bow on the dog give her colour. Her grace and poise strike him as the finest he has ever seen. Her friend in white pique, a few years older, walks beside her there. The young men hurry forward to catch a look at her face. She proves as lovely in face as in form to Raife's eye.
42191-motor-boat-boys-down-the-danube-or:
Motor Boat Boys Down the Danube, or Four Chums Abroad, is a boys tale by Arundel, of four pals on the great river of Europe. It was made in America and put out at Chicago and New York. Its rights were set in law in the mid war years.

A print at its front shows the lads as they pass famed old strong holds on the banks. Its parts open with the four pals in the far land. Then comes word of war at the great town of the Magyars. Risk, doubt from the law, and signs of woes to come fill the first run. A camp on the bank, a storm and its sport, and a mob of the land lead to shots on the river.
42589-homestead:
Arthur G Burgoyne's Homestead, published at Pittsburgh in 1893, gives a complete history of the Homestead struggle. The struggle, in July 1892, set the Carnegie Steel Company against the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers. The publishers set apart five per cent of the net profits toward a monument to the battle of July 6, 1892.

The introduction runs the whole course of the fight, from the lockout at the Carnegie mills to the battle with the Pinkerton guards. Then came the military occupation of Homestead and the trials of labor leaders on capital charges. It ends with the collapse of the Amalgamated lodges for lack of funds, a defeat watched on both sides of the Atlantic.
43046-planet-of-dread:
Planet of Dread is a science fiction story by Murray Leinster, taken from Fantastic Stories of Imagination for May 1962. Moran is a prisoner of the space-yacht Nadine, and her crew has voted to maroon him. The planet chosen is a cloudy world with a small ice-cap.

Moran reads the ice-cap like a report. Water ice means no poison gases in the air. Its small size means wide warm zones where a man might live. The magazine's blurb shows him later on the surface. He cuts apart a yard-long monstrosity with a slash of flame. The thing dies and keeps writhing anyway. Other horrors crawl toward him through the murk. Leinster turns a marooning into a survival trial. The planet's endless terrors test whether a discarded man can stay alive and sane.
43093-coaching-with-anecdotes-of-the-roa:
Lord William Pitt Lennox published 'Coaching, with Anecdotes of the Road' with Hurst and Blackett in London in 1876 and dedicated it to the Duke of Beaufort, president of the Coaching Club. Chapter I runs from ancient charioteers and celebrated whips to the introduction of carriages into England. It gives the state of the roads in 1739 and the flying coach of 1669, with Dean Swift's verses on his journey to Chester.

Later chapters collect dangers of travelling and anecdotes of highwaymen, then slow coaches and fast ones, including the Wonder and the Blenheim. A silver cup presented to a Blenheim driver and public dinners to drivers mark the coaching trade's pride. Coach against rail, Bianconi's cars in Ireland, mails stopped by snowstorms, and coaching in Australia round out the survey.
43119-david-s-little-lad:
Meade wrote David's Little Lad, for Shaw at London in an edition of 1890. Petherick drew the illustrations for the tale. Chapter one is called the story within the story. Gwladys, the teller, must write it down, she opens by saying. The whole country heard of it, and newspapers were full.

High and low, people spoke of the noble deed. A few Welsh miners did that deed, she tells the reader. But the country does not know quite all of it, she owns. She and her mother know the heart history of those ten days. On a sunny afternoon in September 1876 she sat in a nursery window. Her nose flattened against the pane, she gazed down on the sea. What is it to be buried alive, she asked in those days. Meade gives a mine rescue through a girl's heart.
4322-my-three-days-in-gilead:
Elmer U. Hoenshel wrote this travel narrative of three days in Gilead, the biblical land east of the Jordan. His chapters carry him from waiting at Damascus through Bashan, among Bedouins, to Gerasa, up into the mountains, by a watch-tower, and down to the Jordan and its bridge.

Hoenshel writes as a pilgrim and observer, noting the people, camps, and ruins he meets on the road. The book joins scripture geography with firsthand travel, and it suits readers who want a short, vivid account of a Holy Land route. Its charm lies in the pace: three days, closely watched, in an ancient landscape.
43749-the-carpet-from-bagdad:
The Carpet from Bagdad is an adventure novel by Harold MacGrath, published by the Bobbs-Merrill Company of Indianapolis in 1911. Andre Castaigne illustrated it, and MacGrath dedicated it to Robert Hichens. A verse of Kipling's stands at the front.

The hero is George P A Jones, called P A behind the counters. At twenty-eight he is vice-president of Mortimer and Jones. The firm is a great metropolitan house for Oriental rugs and carpets. George is divided against himself. On one side stands his inherent common sense. On the other rises a boundless, roseate imagination of a quixotic kind. That second self pleads with him in luminous rhetoric. The contents promise where it leads him. The Holy Yhiordes, a purloined cable, and a caravan in the desert follow. A Mahomed laughs, offers freedom, and rides alone. Fortune's riddle is solved at last.
4380-under-fire-the-story-of-a-squad:
Henri Barbusse wrote this novel of the First World War from his service in a French infantry squad, translated by Fitzwater Wray. He dedicated it to comrades who fell beside him at Crouy and on Hill 119, in January, May, and September 1915. The contents run from the vision and in the earth to sanctuary, habits, leave, and bombardment.

The squad's life unfolds in trenches, billets, and fatigues, with chapters on the dog, the doorway, big words, and burdens. Barbusse writes without heroics, letting mud, fear, and comradeship speak. Under Fire won the Prix Goncourt, and it remains one of the great novels of the trenches, plain in style and unsparing in truth.
43993-stories-from-the-iliad:
Havell retold these stories from the Iliad for Harrap, first published in February 1908. Havell had written matching story books from Herodotus, Greek tragedy, the Æneid and the Odyssey. A frontispiece shows Athene shooting down from Olympus like a falling star, in Patten Wilson's drawing.

A long quote from Charles Dickens stands at the front of the book. Dickens argues that a nation without fancy and romance can never hold a great place under the sun. The tales that enchanted readers in childhood, he says, enchanted hosts of men and women before them, and Havell offers Homer's war stories in that spirit.
44630-from-a-swedish-homestead:
From a Swedish Homestead, by Selma Lagerlof in the English of Jessie Brochner, was copyrighted in 1901 and issued at Garden City in 1916 by Doubleday, Page. A list of the stories names The Story of a Country House first. Queens at Kungahalla, The Forest Queen, Sigrid Storrade, and Astrid follow. Old Agnete, The Fisherman's Ring, and The Peace of God round out the set.

The country-house story opens on a fine autumn day near the end of the eighteen-thirties. Outside Upsala stood a high yellow two-storied house, alone in a meadow. Virginia creepers climbed its sunny wall and ringed the upper windows. At one window a tall, handsome student drinks his morning coffee. Lagerlof blends saga, legend, and quiet realism in tales drawn from Swedish soil and its old tales.
44648-braddock-road:
Braddock Road is John Kennedy Lacock's history of Braddock's military road of 1755. A map compiled by Lacock in 1912 fronts the article. It runs from Cumberland, Maryland, to Braddock, Pennsylvania. The narrative begins with the general's appointment. On September 24, 1754, the Duke of Cumberland made Edward Braddock captain-general.

Preparations delayed the transports for weeks. Braddock sailed ahead on December 21, 1754. Captain Robert Orme and secretary William Shirley accompanied him. They anchored in Hampton Roads on February 20, 1755. The fleet reached Alexandria by mid-March. Five governors met Braddock in council there on April 14. The advance column had already marched for Wills Creek. Halket's regiment went through Virginia, Dunbar's through Maryland. Want of wagons, horses, and provisions plagued every stage. By May 19 some 2,100 men encamped at Fort Cumberland. The march had taken twenty-seven days for 180 miles.
44816-stanley-in-africa-the-wonderful-di:
Stanley in Africa is a popular life and travel book by James Boyd. Rose of Toronto issued it, with copyright in 1889. Its title promises wonders, finds, and thrilling adventures. Engravings, colour plates, and maps fill the volume. Other travellers, pioneers, and missionaries share its pages. Boyd had written a life of General Grant before. His introduction praises all tales of exploration.

Man seeks the secrets behind mountains, he says. Heroism in pioneers stirs every reader's heart. The New World's unveiling opened the age of exploit. Stanley's African roads are the book's core theme. Such volumes sold by subscription to farm homes. They carried Livingstone's Africa to plain readers. Wonder and moral uplift were their joint stock.
45026-the-four-corners-abroad:
Amy Blanchard takes her Corner girls overseas in The Four Corners Abroad, published by Jacobs at Philadelphia in 1909. A front plate shows Jean perfectly happy with a pigeon on each shoulder. Twenty chapters run from a Fourth of July in Paris to a journey toward the toe of Italy.

Chapter one finds Nan Corner, Mary Lee, and Jo Keyes at Passy on a rainy July afternoon, their walk in the Bois rained off. Jo spots an American flag and recalls the date, sparking patriotic talk of Bunker Hill and Yorktown. Later chapters cover Bastille Day, housekeeping in Paris, a glimpse of Spain, and a fiesta. London, Munich, mountain travel, and a fairy play follow before the girls head south.
46124-the-copperhead:
Harold Frederic wrote this novel, The Copperhead, printed in New York in 1893. Fourteen chapters carry the tale, most of them named for Abner Beech, its central figure. Jeff's Mutiny, Antietam, and an election and its bonfire stand in the list. Esther's visit, a fire, and the conquest of Abner drive the back half toward a close called Finis.

The narrator tells the tale as a grown man looking back. He went to live with Farmer Beech at six or seven, and the old farm-house burned over their heads on his thirteenth birthday. Abner Beech was a stalwart, thick-shouldered man with stern hazel eyes and a beard in iron-grey billows. He was a citizen of weight, first with a mowing-machine, and a pillar of the church before the matter of the lightning-rods.
47149-the-care-of-the-dead:
London print of 1916 holds this account of care for war dead graves. Eyre and Spottiswoode issued the short, grave piece. It opens in a graveyard west of Vimy in France. There 1320 French soldiers and more than 600 English lie buried.

A French officer told the English, we leave you our trenches and dead. An English keeper tends French and English graves alike with care. A French woman in mourning brings white flowers to one grave. She joins an English burial party and leaves her flowers there in the grave. Eyre and Spottiswoode printed the account at London in 1916.
48252-motor-matt-s-daring-rescue-or-the-:
Motor Matt rides again in Motor Stories number 11 from Street and Smith, New York, dated May 8, 1909 at five cents. Weekly numbers cost $2.50 a year by subscription in that day, the masthead states in fine print. Sixteen chapters make up the tale, with short extras on fortune and rabbit hunting at the tail.

Matt King, called Mile-a-minute Matt by the boys of his western town, stands first in the cast list. Carl Pretzel, a cheerful German lad, and Dick Ferral, a Canadian boy from the King's navy, ride at his side. A plate shows Dick crying step lively as Matt helps a girl into the car at the start. Heads promise the disappearance of Helen Brady, a fight, daring work, and Helen's ordeal in the run.
48560-scho-ne-aussicht-a-journal-of-our-:
Louise Spilker wrote Schone Aussicht, A Journal of Our Trip Abroad, printed at New York in 1901 with pictures by the author. A poem by Ella Wheeler Wilcox heads the book. The poem urges the artist to work on and heed no sneers. Chapter One starts with a note of care for the reader.

Spilker's journal form keeps the trip in day order. The German title means a fine view. The tale is a home travel record for kin and friends more than a guide book. Verse, prints, and plain talk mix in its pages. Readers get the feel of an American trip abroad at the turn of the age, seen through one woman's eye and hand.
48596-take-it-from-dad:
George Livermore wrote this book of letters from a father to his son, published by Macmillan in 1920. The first letter answers Ted, who has written from Exeter asking if he is a failure and whether he can have a factory job instead.

Dad's answer is yes to failure, and I can but I won't to the job. He tells the boy his trouble begins with h and ends with k, homesickness, and that a big frog in Lynn is a small one among five hundred boys. He confesses his own shrinking at a Binghamton shoe factory making fifty thousand pairs a day to his eight thousand. Fathers and sons get plain, funny advice in letter form.
48990-old-dad:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott wrote a tale printed at New York in 1919. Eight printings ran in the first three months alone. The book falls in two parts, each of three chapters. It opens on a momentous day for Daphne Bretton.

Daphne has just been thrown out of college. She bursts into her father's book lined room in a strange city. Till that day she had neither known nor liked him well. The name Old-Dad slips from her lips as she flings out her news. Her young father's face goes white as hers. What for, he gasps. Twice her lips open and shut in pain, and at last she tells him the charge.
49436-joseph-conrad:
A short critical life of Joseph Conrad by Hugh Walpole. Henry Holt published it at New York. Walpole divides his study into four parts. Biography comes first, then the novelist and the poet. A closing section weighs romance and realism. Bibliographies and an index complete the volume.

Walpole argues that Conrad's life feeds his art directly. Three backgrounds frame that art: Poland, the sea, and England. Conrad was born in the Ukraine in 1857.
