Exile to Vologda followed his father's part in a Polish rising. His mother and then his father died in his boyhood. A compelling impulse took him to sea in 1874. He mastered English and earned a master's certificate. Almayer's Folly opened his writing life in 1895.
49589-the-switzerland-of-america-lehigh-: The Switzerland of America is a plate book for the Lehigh Valley Railroad, with rights in eighteen ninety-seven. Its pages are full page black and white views of spots past that road in the east of two states. Past its front note the text is but the short names past the plates. Views run from a curve of the road and a famed school to falls, glens, and the great falls of the north.
49754-what-do-you-read:
Boyd Ellanby wrote What Do You Read, a tale printed in Other Worlds in March 1953. Malcolm Smith drew the pictures. The teaser says writers dreamed of a plot machine, but the Script-Lab machines did far more: they wrote the stories themselves.

Herbert, an aging staff writer at the Bureau of Public Entertainment, rides the moving sidewalks to lunch with his chief. He is well paid but cannot afford a taxi. On the Airway a young cripple is pushed through the railing and falls to the street. Herbert wonders whether he can make a plot of it. Ludwig receives him with the recorder shut off, and the talk turns grave.
49787-love-s-golden-thread:
Edith Kenyon published Love's Golden Thread with Partridge of Paternoster Row in 1905, with six illustrations. Her motto comes from Archbishop Trench: through life's darkest woof there runs, enwoven from above, the golden thread of love.

The contents follow Doris. A terrible wrong opens the story, and a pencil note carries it forward. Bernard searches for Doris, and Doris is alone in London. Friends in need, new work, and work shared with Alice Sinclair follow. Conscience money, a powerful temptation, and the great renunciation raise the stakes. A welcome legacy arrives near the end, as the contents frankly promise. Kenyon wrote a shelf of such tales for the religious market. Her plots run on providence, and the thread of the title is the plot itself, visible to faith before it is visible to Doris.
52261-a-record-of-st-cybi-s-church-holyh:
A record of St Cybi's Church at Holyhead gathers the church's history and a sermon preached after its restoration in 1879. Arthur Penrhyn Stanley, Dean of Westminster, gave that sermon. A south view shows the chancel aisle added in 1897, in the Jubilee year of Queen Victoria.

A new south aisle seats fifty or sixty worshippers, given in memory of Mr and Mrs W O Stanley of Penrhos. An east window honours Mr Watson of the City of Dublin Company. The Stanley kin, the Owens of Penrhos, kept close ties to the church for ages. Ruskin is quoted on the holy headland, its red light glaring through storm over the sea.
52453-joseph-conrad:
Hugh Walpole wrote a short life and study of Joseph Conrad, issued in New York in 1916. Walpole holds that Conrad's own life went straight into his art, so the critic must know it. Three grounds shape that art: Poland, the sea, and an English country home.

Conrad was born on 6th December 1857 in the Ukraine, in the south of Poland. His father was banished to Vologda in 1862 for his part in a Polish rising, and both parents died by 1870. Conrad went to sea in 1874, landed in England in May 1878 with no English, and left the sea in 1894 to write.
52824-the-story-of-a-loaf-of-bread:
Wood, Drapers Professor of Agriculture at Cambridge, wrote The Story of a Loaf of Bread for the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature in 1913. The little book follows one loaf from field to table. Its title page copies a design of John Siberch, the earliest known Cambridge printer.

The story runs through wheat, harvest, milling, and baking. An agriculture professor explains what each stage does and why the loaf costs what it costs. The manuals series packed university learning into pocket volumes for general readers. Bread was the right subject for 1913. The price of the loaf was a live political question, and free trade had been fought over it for a decade. Wood gives the science plainly, and lets the reader draw the moral.
53701-uncle-sam-abroad:
J E Conner wrote Uncle Sam Abroad, with illustrations by Clyde J Newman, issued at Chicago and New York by Rand, McNally and Company with copyright in nineteen hundred. A front plate shows Uncle Sam carrying a suitcase. Five lectures and an appendix fill the book. A frame tale opens it, The Professor Has an Idea. Professor Loyal of a university holds that the average American knows little of his government abroad.

Lecture one treats the State Department. Lectures two and three treat the consular service, its officers and its duties. Lecture four treats the diplomatic service. Lecture five treats Uncle Sam and expansion, a hot topic in nineteen hundred. The appendix prints tables of diplomatic and consular posts and a synopsis of commercial treaties. Citizens get a plain guide to how the United States speaks to the world.
53901-the-merman-and-the-figure-head:
Two tales for young readers share one Philadelphia volume from J B Lippincott and Co in 1874. Mary D Nauman writes Eva's Adventures in Shadow-Land, and Clara F Guernsey writes The Merman and the Figure-Head. The joint title page calls the pair Adventures in Shadow-Land and notes that both tales carry pictures.

Guernsey's tale starts in Salem, where merchant Isaac Torrey names his fine new brig The Sea-nymph. His old clerk, Ichabod Sterns, frowns at the name as heathen for a ship from a strict Christian town. Six chapters then move from the Sea Kingdom to a bewitched lover and a dream by Lucy Peabody. The talk on the wharf sets up a sea tale with a touch of magic.
55830-peggy-on-the-road:
Peggy on the Road, by Virginia Hughes, is one of the Peggy Lane Theater Stories for young readers. Grosset and Dunlap printed it in New York in 1963, with pictures by Sergio Leone. A front plate shows Peggy reading with mounting conviction and assurance.

Peggy Lane, a young actress, soaks her aching feet in hot water and bath salts at the Gramercy Arms, a rooming house for actresses near Gramercy Park. Half a dozen hopeful girls in twin rooms share the daily ritual they call cocktail hour. The contents promise the break of a lifetime, tryouts, Peggy turning detective, a one eyed giant, a star who comes back, and a curtain going up.
56207-strive-and-succeed-or-the-progress:
Horatio Alger tells Strive and Succeed, or The Progress of Walter Conrad, for Hurst in New York, in a uniform boys' series priced on the advertisement page. Alger dedicates the volume to his young friends Isabella and Edwin. A long series list names dozens of his titles, from Bound to Rise to Tony the Tramp.

A preface dated at New York on October 1, 1872, says the tale first ran as a serial in Young Israel, a juvenile magazine. Readers of Strong and Steady will find Walter Conrad's later career here, plus Joshua Drummond's adventures after fleeing home. Alger defends Walter's success as a young teacher in the West with real cases he knows. Chapter one puts the stout, gentlemanly Walter, not yet sixteen, on a Wisconsin train with a carpetbag holding all his clothing.
56284-the-legend-of-kupirri-or-the-red-k:
W A Cawthorne set down a short Aboriginal legend from the Port Lincoln tribe in South Australia. The book was printed in Adelaide in the year given in Roman numerals as MDCCCLVIII. Its title names Kupirri, a huge red kangaroo said to have eaten all who tried to spear him. Two famed hunters, Pilla and Inda, stand at the heart of the tale.

Inside, the hunters track Kupirri to Mount Nilarro and kill him after a hard fight. They find lost friends alive in the beast, heal them, and feast in turn. Notes link the tale to huge old bones and to a pamphlet by C W Schurmann from 1846.
5720-a-shropshire-lad:
Housman's Shropshire Lad gathers short lyrics of youth, love, loss, and the English countryside, introduced in this edition by William Stanley Braithwaite in 1919. The introduction praises how the poems wear the attire of reality in the simplest speech, yet rise into sheer loveliness of spirit. Shropshire hills, lanes, soldiers, and seasons give the poems their setting, while parting and death give them their ache.

Readers meet plain diction carrying deep feeling, with soldiers marching, lovers parting, and young men facing a short life. The poems are brief enough to read one at a time, and they repay slow reading aloud. Housman's collection remains a favorite for those who love English lyric poetry that says hard truths in clear, musical lines.
57316-west-point-an-intimate-picture-of-:
Robert Charlwood Richardson, a captain of cavalry who had taught English at West Point, wrote an intimate picture of the national military academy, issued in 1917. A foreword by Hugh Scott, chief of staff, notes that cadets were about to sail for the battlefields of France. The book is dedicated to the corps of cadets.

Early chapters give the academy's first hundred years and the building of its stone halls. Later ones show cadet life from the first hard weeks, nicknamed Beast Barracks, through drill, study, and sport. He treats discipline of mind, growth of muscle, and the forming of moral fiber. Scott calls the corps the heirs of a century of honour.
58426-the-speeches-table-talk-of-the-pro:
Stanley Lane-Poole chooses and turns sayings of the Prophet in a Macmillan volume from London dated 1882, with notes and an opening essay. A Throne Verse in full capitals heads the book before the introduction starts in earnest. Lane-Poole states his aim at the start: the most enduring words in a form the general reader can take up.

Folk talk, write, and preach much about Mohammad of which a slight acquaintance would show the absurdity, Lane-Poole writes. No one would dare treat the classics of Europe in such a loose way without swift exposure, he adds. The book lets any reader judge stock fallacies on the prophet and his creed at the least cost of effort. Public orations and private table-talk stand side by side in the chosen set.
58836-dagonet-abroad:
George Sims published Dagonet Abroad in London in 1895, inscribing it to Count Albert Edward von Armfelt, his constant companion on the trip. Sims wrote under the Dagonet name for light journalism and also authored Mary Jane's Memoirs. The trip begins in Bordeaux and the Basque country.

Chapters travel from Biarritz to Burgos, then Madrid, Seville, Granada, and Cordova, with a chapter of Spanish impressions. The party crosses to Algiers, then returns through Monte Carlo, Genoa, Florence, Rome, and Naples. Readers get a chatty Victorian travel diary, city by city, from a popular newspaper humorist seeing Spain, Africa, and Italy in one sweep.
59354-gloria-a-girl-and-her-dad:
Lilian Garis wrote a tale of a girl and her father that Grosset and Dunlap copyrighted in 1923. Gloria Doane has a father and no mother. Her friend Tom Whitely has a mother and no father. That shared lack, the book says, bound them from the days when both first toddled off to school in the back room of a fancy goods store.

Gloria has red cheeks and black flashing eyes under a floppy white hat. Tom is tall, with a saddle of fine freckles and a soft, musical voice. Few folk see his worth, for his alert mind flashes out only in free moments. The chapters take the pair to Turtle Cove, Crystal Springs, and Echo Park. An uncle, a hunt, and a quest for a tweed coat fill the middle. The tale ends with a trapping and a rescue.
59381-simple-plumbing-repairs-for-the-ho:
Farmers' Bulletin Number 2202 from the Department of Agriculture teaches homeowners and farmers to make minor plumbing repairs themselves and save money and delay. The revised edition is dated December 1972.

Dripping faucets are the most common problem, and a new washer is normally all that is required. The bulletin walks through faucets and valves, leaks in pipes and tanks, water hammer, and frozen pipes, then water closets and clogged drains. It warns that extensive work needs local authorization and a licensed plumber. Copies sold for 15 cents from the Superintendent of Documents at Washington. The bulletin supersedes an earlier Farmers' Bulletin on repairs in the home.
59907-the-riviera-of-the-corniche-road:
The Riviera of the Corniche Road is a travel book by Sir Frederick Treves, published by Cassell and Company in 1921. Treves was serjeant-surgeon to the King and wrote other travel books, among them The Other Side of the Lantern. His own 92 photographs illustrate this one.

The road runs east from Nice along the cliffs. Treves walks the reader through Nice first: the Promenade des Anglais, the old town, and its siege. Cimiez and the convent of St Pons follow. Vence, Grasse, and Cagnes each get their chapters. Cap Ferrat, Eze, and the harbour and rock of Monaco come next. Monte Carlo gets three chapters, including its diversions. La Turbie, Roquebrune, and Mentone close the road. Sospel, inland, ends the book. The volume dresses a surgeon's holiday notes as a guide to the coast road.
60474-the-last-travels-of-ida-pfeiffer-i:
Oscar Pfeiffer prepared The Last Travels of Ida Pfeiffer for Harper and Brothers at New York in 1861, in a version by H W Dulcken. Ida Pfeiffer died of an illness caught in Mauritius after leaving Madagascar. Her son learned of her death at Buenos Ayres and found her papers waiting at Rio de Janeiro.

Her last wish was that he arrange the journal of her Madagascar voyage. He left the text as little altered as duty allowed. A memoir of the author opens the volume. Chapters start from Vienna through Linz, Salzburg, and Munich, with a visit to Alexander von Humboldt at Berlin. Holland and Amsterdam follow. The Madagascar journey forms the heart of the last travels.
60514-about-algeria-algiers-tlemc-en-con:
About Algeria is a travel book on the towns of Algeria named in its title. Algiers, Tlemcen, Constantine, Biskra, and Timgad mark its route across the land. A note at the front tells how the print form was set, with notes moved to sit by the parts that call them.

Full page prints are marked by their word frames, set at the nearest break in the text. Small faults of the press have been fixed in the copy. The book takes the reader town by town, with the look of streets and ruins, the past of each place, and the life of its folk. It serves as a guide for the guest and a sketch for the home reader.
60911-the-wonderland-of-trinidad:
The Wonderland of Trinidad was issued by the Barber Asphalt Company of Philadelphia to praise the island and its asphalt lake. The native name of the island, Iere, is given as the land of the humming bird. Trinidad lies not far north of the equator and belongs to Great Britain in the book telling.

The asphalt lake stands at the center, called the marvel of centuries and a subject of study for men of science. The text recalls the ships that passed the straits: Columbus on his third voyage, Raleigh and the buccaneers, and Nelson hunting the French fleet. Port of Spain houses and tropical scenes fill the pictures. The book is part travel wonder, part sales piece for the black gold of the lake.
61013-the-fastest-gun-dead:
The Fastest Gun Dead, a story by Julian Grow, was printed in Worlds of If in March 1961. Its headnote gives the joke away: the skeleton had the fastest draw west of the Pecos, too bad he was such a lousy shot. A big man stands in a saloon door, broad of shoulder and slim of hip, his Stetson crimped Texas style. Dust from the streets of Dos Cervezas Pequenas swirls about his chaps.

His slate grey eyes sweep the crowd at the bar and stop at one man. I want you, Dirty Jake, he says, flat as tempered steel. Dirty Jake shoots him into doll rags, naturally, the narrator adds. Dirty Jake, it turns out, is the most feared ribbon clerk in the territory. Grow mixes the western with the weird, turning the classic showdown on its head. The tale plays the gunfighter legend for dry, strange comedy.
6103-tales-of-the-road:
Charles N. Crewdson dedicates Tales of the Road to Alex C. Ritchey, salesman and friend, and opens with the claim that the salesman is the steam, and a big part of the engine too, that makes business move. His contents promise the square deal, clerks, cranks and touches, and social arts as salesmen's assets.

Tricks of the trade, the helping hand, first experiences, tactics in selling, cutting prices, canceled orders, and credit men follow. Winning the customer's good will, salesmen's don'ts, merchants met on the road, and hearts behind the order book close the book. Crewdson writes selling as craft and character.
6132-a-man-of-samples-something-about-th:
Wm. H. Maher opens A Man of Samples with a midnight departure: when do you start, Tom, at midnight, good-by, sock it to them, send fat orders. The traveling man is off on a wedding tour, and the narrator, a stock clerk and house salesman for three years, has agreed to take his place for one trip.

As the hour nears, his courage sinks, and he heartily wishes he had never consented. Success on the road gains him nothing, since he means not to continue there, while failure might make his house place less secure. Maher turns one reluctant trip into portraits of men met on the road, with humor and worry.
6150-the-iliad:
Homer's Iliad appears here rendered into English blank verse by Edward, Earl of Derby, in twenty-four books. The preface recalls that in spring 1862, at friends' request, Derby printed for private circulation a small volume of translations, including the first book of the Iliad.

Competent judges praised his attempt to infuse into an almost literal version something of the spirit and simplicity of the great original, encouraging him to continue. The work gave him unfailing and growing interest in intervals of more urgent business, and he finished it with regret. Derby's Iliad prizes fidelity with poetic ease.
61756-sphere-of-the-never-dead:
Sphere of the Never-Dead is a science fiction story by Sam Carson, first published in Planet Stories in the summer of 1940. Its hero is Bob Winslow, a young physicist at Kerla Research, about to be made director at twenty-six for his work on the Decka light stream and his electronoscope. His roommate Jim Kenley, an auditor, lives for sport.

On a stormy night Bob crosses to Jim's car with a growing sense of being followed by something invisible and invincible. Lightning silhouettes the city, and then Jim is catapulted from the car by unseen hands and Bob himself is gripped by absolute cold and plunged into a white, soundless world. The magazine's blurb names the stakes: the three brains of Taval have decreed that Kenley must die and enter death-in-life. The story is pulp time-strata adventure in its purest early form.
61817-rollo-learning-to-read:
Rollo Learning to Read, by Jacob Abbott, is the second volume of the Rollo Books, Abbott's famed series for young children. Fourteen volumes make the set, running from Rollo Learning to Talk to the Rollo studies of water, air, fire, and sky. This new edition was revised by the author.

A notice to parents explains Abbott's method. Most books for beginners, he argues, fail by cramping themselves into words of one syllable, which makes the style quaint and harder to follow. Abbott instead writes in natural language and trusts the child's interest to pull him through the hard words. Stories of Rollo at home give the small reader matter worth reading aloud and repeating to brothers and sisters. The first edition was entered for copyright in 1855.
62269-gypsy-coppersmiths-in-liverpool-an:
Andreas, called Mui Shuko, sketches Gypsy Coppersmiths in Liverpool and Birkenhead, in a Liverpool print of 1913. Henry Young and Sons made the book. A photograph of Vola fronts the text. Two odd, warm gift notes open the pages.

One note makes amends to a friend vexed when rail staff barred his donkey from a dog ticket. One thanks a friend for Luke and scrambled eggs in hours of low spirits. A table then maps how the Gypsies of the book link by blood. Tomo, Gunia, and Grantsha, born in 1825, head the lines. Their children and grandchildren fill the chart, chiefs and wives in turn. Andreas writes as one of the kin he maps.
63783-savage-galahad:
Bryce Walton sinks into alien thought in Savage Galahad, from the Winter 1946 issue of Planet Stories. The head blurb hails the beast: tons of sinuous muscle, buried in fetid Venusian slime, he knew how to survive. Equipped with an ageless brain and lightning instincts, he also knew how to die.

The tale opens inside the creature. He stirs slightly, his ponderously long body trembling with the rhythm of the tall pale watergrass. Dim and monstrous shadows float past, then spurt in frenzied speed to devour or be devoured. An alien organism has come to his world. Its strange radiations pierce his brain in waves of bizarre beauty. In her confused mind he reads a far world, symbolized as Earth. She faces certain death, disoriented with terror, and names his world Venus, planet of the morning.
642-the-altar-of-the-dead:
Henry James writes of grief and memory in this short novel, published in 1916 in Martin Secker's edition. George Stransom dislikes lean anniversaries, yet keeps one rite each year. It marks the death of Mary Antrim, the girl who was to have been his bride and died of fever before the wedding. No priest and no altar made him widowed; loss alone did.

James writes with quiet, measured prose, following Stransom's private altar of the dead through years of remembrance. The tale asks whom we honor and whom we forgive. It endures as a tender study of mourning, where one man's faithfulness outlasts every other love.
65086-world-of-the-mad:
Poul Anderson's World of the Mad ran in Imagination for February 1951. The headnote says Langdon had found immortality on the planet Tanith, and naturally wanted his wife to share it, if he could keep her from going insane first. Langdon walks through curling purple mists, hearing voices sing in high unhuman tones and a crystal tree chime its glass leaves. Blind beautiful faces mouth at him from the fog.

Flowers of crystalline petals bloom and die as he passes, some reaching hungrily for him. Even after two hundred years he is not sure what is real. Compasses fail on Tanith and his sense of direction rotates crazily, yet long habit takes him home. A ghost city of the old folk of Tanith grows out of the mist, complete this time, under three hurtling moons. Anderson writes the tale as lucid delirium.
65304-the-road:
Hilaire Belloc wrote The Road, printed at Manchester in 1923 for the British Reinforced Concrete Engineering Company. The book argues the case for roads built by design in concrete. It opens with a rational discourse of 1675 on the highways of England, shown as an old title page to prove the antiquity of the road problem. That tract called the old way of mending a cheat and promised a firm road with no deep ruts, holes, or loose stones.

Belloc's chapters treat the road in general: the origin of roads, the crossing of marsh and water, and the like heads. He sets the haphazard road against the road of design, and reads history in the ways men have made. The book is both a history of the road and a piece of advocacy for the concrete way of building it.
65625-the-first-of-may-a-new-version-of-:
Anna Harriet Drury retells a famous ballad in The First of May, a new version from William Pickering in London in 1851, here in its sixth edition. Drury had written Friends and Fortune, named on her title page. Her subject is Prince Albert and the Great Exhibition, recast in the marching stanzas of Macaulay's style.

Albert swears by the Cinque Ports to make an exhibition never seen before and names the opening day, the First of May. Letters go out worldwide; parcels bundle in by waggon, train, and Pickford's vans from Russia, France, and the far republic across the Atlantic. The commission leads a weary life, unable to choose a building or find a site while pamphlets, prophecies, and warnings choke the prince's desk. Newspapers threaten that the tickets will not sell.
65641-dad:
Albert Payson Terhune writes a war novel in Dad, copyrighted in 1914 by W J Watt and Company of New York, with a frontispiece by W D Goldbeck. Terhune dedicates the story lovingly to the Sunnybank people. Thirty-four chapters run from disgrace and outcast through fourteen years later to Sergeant Dadd, the Chickahominy, a character called General Dadd and the prodigal father.

The first chapter opens on a plaza under white sun-glare, where a crack regiment marches in the regimentals of the late forties. Mexican musicians wrestle with Columbia, the Gem of the Ocean, an irony attributed to Major-General Winfield Scott.
65841-the-lost-dryad:
The Lost Dryad is a short fairy tale by Frank R. Stockton, printed at Hillacre in a run of one thousand copies. Stockton dictated the tale in 1901 for Mrs. Frederick Gotthold, who had long loved his tale Old Pipes and the Dryad. No second copy was made at the time, and the small hand-bound book stayed with her for ten years.

After Stockton died in April 1902, Mrs. Gotthold gave the tale to the Eastern Branch of the United Workers of Greenwich. The group sold the rights in 1911 and used the funds to print the book. Cash from sales was set aside to build a club-house and play ground for poor village children.
65944-bread:
Bread, by Charles Norris, was published in New York in 1923. Norris had also written Salt and Brass, a novel of marriage. He dedicates Bread to the working women of America. Three books, with many chapters, make up the long novel.

Book one opens in a music lesson. Mrs Sturgis taps the ivory keys of the piano with her pencil as she counts the beat. One and two and three and four, she counts, again and again. Her little pupils grow nervous at the tapping, and sometimes are upset completely. Now she abruptly breaks off her counting. Readers get a Norris novel of a working woman life, set against wages, hunger, and marriage, by a writer known for plain studies of American domestic strain.
65998-the-witch-s-head:
The Witch Head, by Rider Haggard, is here in a twenty sixth thousand printing, published in London, with sixteen full page illustrations by Charles Kerr. Haggard other works listed include Dawn, King Solomon Mines, She, and Jess. Contents run to two books of many chapters.

Book one opens with Ernest appearance, then Reginald Cardus, a misanthrope. Old Dum Ness, boys together, and Eva promise follow. Jeremy falls in love, Ernest is indiscreet, and a garden idyl comes next. Eva finds something, and what Eva found follows. Deep waters, and deeper yet, mark the middle. Cardus unfolds his plans, a goodbye is said, and Ernest gets into trouble. Book two opens with my poor Eva. Readers get an early Haggard novel of love and trouble in England, before the African romances made him famous.
66108-a-gloucestershire-lad-at-home-and-:
F W Harvey wrote A Gloucestershire Lad at Home and Abroad. Sidgwick and Jackson issued it at London in 1917. Four impressions ran within seven months. The first came in September 1916. The book goes to comrades dead in foreign fields. Living comrades who fight on share the gift.

A Song of Gloucestershire opens the verse set. Ballades and songs of Minsterworth follow. Cricket, triolets, and a Song of the Road fill the home side. War pieces crowd the later pages here. A Present from Flanders and If We Return stand there. Gonnehmen and The Rest Farm name trench places. To the Kaiser speaks straight at the foe. Sergeant Finch and the company cook get portraits. A soldier-poet's songs join orchard and lane to trench and gun in one small, loved book.
66204-the-cyclopedia-of-the-colored-bapt:
The Cyclopedia of the Colored Baptists of Alabama, Their Leaders and Their Work, is a reference book by Charles Octavius Boothe. Boothe was also the author of Plain Theology for Plain People, as his title page notes. It was published at Birmingham in eighteen ninety five, with a portrait of Boothe as frontispiece. An index of illustrations runs to many pages of portraits and churches.

Pastors, lay leaders, women workers, churches, and Selma University are all pictured and profiled. In the age of Jim Crow, Black Baptists built a dense world of churches and schools in Alabama. Boothe's cyclopedia preserves names and faces that white records ignored. For church and family history in the state, it is a prime source.
66328-planet-of-dread:
Dwight Swain wrote Planet of Dread, a science fiction story printed in Imagination in February 1954. The planet Lysor, surrounded by its many suns, scorns Federation rule and plots the destruction of the galaxy. Agent Craig Nesom comes in a starship to stop it. The story opens in a walled pit. A terrified Baemae woman comes through the gate while the Kukzubas barons and their ladies press close about the rail, eager for the games.

On his dais Lord Zenaor banters with Vydys, a dark beauty the barons call cruel behind her back. She prefers the Baemae in their proper role, as prey. Zenaor warns that her passion for pain is driving the serfs to rebellion; many have already flown south on their discs. Swain writes space opera of the pulp school: wicked courts and captive peoples.
68325-nomad:
Nomad, by Wesley Long, ran as a serial in Astounding Science-Fiction across the winter of 1944 and 1945. Drawings by Orban go with the tale. Guy Maynard of the Terran Space Patrol walks out of the Bureau of Exploration Building at Sahara Base and straight into trouble.

Trouble takes the shape of a MacMillan pistol in the clawlike hand of a Martian. The muzzle sits dead-center on the pit of Maynard's stomach. Sahara Base is as guarded a place as any on Earth, which makes the ambush a shock. Maynard runs through the moves he had rehearsed in his mind for just such a moment. In those daydreams he always won, by force or by marching the foe off at gunpoint. Reality now tests the script.
68388-how-to-thought-read:
How to Thought Read, by James Coates, is a manual on psychic arts. Hay Nisbet of London and Glasgow issued the one shilling book in eighteen ninety three. Coates taught mental science and hygiene and wrote How to Mesmerise. The full title promises the strange and mystic in daily life.

Contents cover hypnotic, mesmeric, and psychic states and mind reading of all kinds. Thought transference, psychometry, clairvoyance, and spiritualism stand in the list. Chapter one treats sleepwalking, dreams, warnings, and double consciousness at length. Chapter two turns to clairvoyance, or soul sight, and how to grow it. Chapter three sorts cases of clairvoyance with strange stories as proof.
69171-mother-hubbard-s-cupboard-recipes-:
Mother Hubbard’s Cupboard holds recipes gathered by a church ladies’ group in Rochester. The Young Ladies’ Society of the First Baptist Church made the book. Scrantom, Wetmore and Company issued this fourth edition in eighteen hundred eighty seven. Twenty thousand copies had gone out when this set was printed.

Fifty cents by mail bought the book from the Rochester group. Soups lead the bill of fare, with beef soup at the head. A soup bone boils a day ahead in that first plain rule. Macaroni soup from Ida Satterlee follows in signed form. Each cook signs her own dish through the whole book. Fish, vegetables, bread, and pies fill the mid pages in turn. Cakes take the largest share of the sweet back half. Pickles, canned fruit, salads, and drinks close the full store.
6970-the-history-of-a-mouthful-of-bread:
Jean Mace traces a mouthful of bread through the body, showing its effect on the organization of men and animals. Translated from the eighth French edition by Missus Alfred Gatty, the little work had been adopted by the University Commission at Paris among their prize books. Gatty admits she sat down with no special love for the subject as fare for young people, yet became a thorough convert to the author's way of teaching it.

She argues such a study, pursued as Mace pursues it, proves most useful and most desirable for the young. The book follows food from mouth to muscle and mind, turning digestion into a clear story. It aims to make physiology lively, plain, and memorable for school readers.
6987-five-little-peppers-abroad:
Margaret Sidney continues the Pepper family in Five Little Peppers Abroad, answering friends who begged for more of their good times. Readers had asked for the stories Polly told to keep the children happy in the hard days of the little brown house. They also wanted a book of plays and exploits that could not fit the main history. Parents joined the young in urging a volume that would show the influences shaping the children's lives.

Sidney complied, giving a detailed account meant to throw stronger light on family life in that home. The book gathers tales and games from the Peppers abroad, with illustrations by Fanny Cory. It is a warm family volume, meant for all who loved the five little Peppers and wished to stay longer with them.
7132-the-purple-land-being-the-narrative:
W H Hudson tells The Purple Land as the narrative of Richard Lamb's adventures in the Banda Oriental of South America, in a second edition of 1904 illustrated by Keith Henderson. The preface recalls a first issue in 1885, by Sampson Low, in two slim volumes under the longer, enigmatic title The Purple Land That England Lost. A purple land, Hudson notes, may be found in almost any region, and people count gains, not losses.

A few newspaper notices appeared, and one or two serious journals reviewed the book unfavorably under travels and geography, but the public would not buy, and it fell into oblivion. There it might have slept nineteen years or forever, since a book's sleep is apt to be unawakening. The second edition revived a South American romance of love, wandering, and politics.
74231-the-story-of-the-iliad:
Alfred Church, lately a professor of Latin in London, retold The Story of the Iliad for school use; the Macmillan edition carries a 1905 copyright and this printing of 1920. Church turns Homer's poem into plain prose chapters for young readers, with guides to saying the Greek names. Twenty-three chapters carry the siege of Troy from first cause to last ransom.

The first chapter, The Quarrel, begins before the war: Helen, fairest of women, leaves Sparta with Paris, and the Greek chiefs gather a hundred thousand men to win her back. After nine years of siege, the camp quarrels over spoil from a sacked town and the priest's daughter given to Agamemnon. Later chapters follow the deeds of Diomed, the embassy to Achilles, the death of Patroclus, and the slaying of Hector. Readers get the whole arc of the Iliad in brisk English made for the classroom.
74793-what-happened-to-tad:
Mary E Ropes wrote What Happened to Tad, a tale of a boy ground down at home. The Religious Tract Society issued the book in London. Ropes had written Karl Jansen’s Find and Two Brave Boys before. Tad Poole, nicknamed Tadpole by his friends, opens the tale in strife.

His father James backs the new wife in all things at home. She beats small Bert and boxes Nell’s ears for slight faults. Her own great baby wants for nothing in that house. Tad works as a grocer’s lad at four shillings a week. Foot sore and worn, he still keeps a good heart in him. Plots of revenge, a flight, and the open sea follow fast. Jeremiah Jackson and faithful Phil cross his hard road in time. Tables turn at last on the cruel house he fled.
75071-bad-and-mad:
Bad and Mad is a western story by Tuttle, author of Dangling Doom. The tale opens at a desert water hole. A man on his knees is ordered to put his hands up by a stranger with a rifle.

The stranger wears a badge on his vest, and the two men are as alike as two peas. Both are smooth shaven, slightly grizzled, and lean, in much the same clothes. Each knows the other at once, and each names the other with astonishment. They are brothers, one on each side of the law, and neither trusts the other any more than he ever did. The held-up man misquotes Burns on seeing ourselves as others see us. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
75376-edaville-railroad:
Linwood Moody wrote 'Edaville Railroad: The Cranberry Belt,' published by Ellis Atwood at South Carver, Massachusetts, in 1947. His opening joke sets the scale: the Edaville Railroad is eighteen hundred acres long and only two feet wide. Atwood's Edaville, Moody explains, is the biggest privately owned cranberry business in the world, with 210 acres of actual bog.

Moody first stacks up the local firsts: Carver harvests 100,000 barrels a year from 2,800 acres of bog, fifteen per cent of the whole world's crop. Edaville itself grows nearly 10,000 barrels of the sour little berries each year. Photographs by Cyrus Hosmer, Moody, and Atwood show the narrow gauge line at work, including an early freight train. Railroad fan John Holt sits at the throttle of Monson engine number 4 in that picture.
75646-the-astounding-crime-on-torrington:
William Gillette wrote a crime narrative published by Harper in 1927, framed as the Pentecost episode in a most audacious criminal career. The recital, taken down and set forth, divides into seven parts. Part one leads up to an arrangement between Andrew Howard Barnes and Horace McClintock. Gillette was the actor who defined Sherlock Holmes on the American stage. His crime story uses the theatre's timing.

The Torrington Road crime unfolds as a recital rather than a plain novel. Gillette also wrote plays and Holmes adaptations. Harper issued the book in New York and London. Its seven part structure mimics a dossier of depositions. The astounding tone is part showman's wink.
76082-one-jump-ahead:
Ray Humphreys, author of Not of the Card, wrote this Western story of a second chance. Manuel Perez comes early to the sheriff's office, hobbling on his wooden leg. He has served three years in the big house for rustling calves and is out on parole. His place has fallen to ruin, he has no money, and he reminds Sheriff Joe Cook of a promise: help him when he came out.

Cook and his deputy, Shorty McKay, take him in kindly. The sheriff allows that Perez got off light with five to seven years, and that his rustling days had better be done. He offers to ring Earl Wettengel for work as a sheep-herder, or Art Wachter if that fails. Perez swears he will stay on the square. The title hints the law, and Perez, both plan to keep one jump ahead.
76385-a-golden-thread:
A Golden Thread, a tale by Marian Isabel Hurrell, was printed in London in 1927 by the Epworth Press. The book opens with a girl of fourteen who carries a long, bulky envelope up to a man in a deck chair. She asks if he is Mr. Charlton, editor of Sunny Hours.

The girl is Eileen Bannister, and she writes stories of her own. Charlton is on a rest break by doctor's orders, in a quiet spot far off the beaten track. Eileen found him through his landlady, Mrs. Stannard, and begs five minutes of his time. The parts ahead name Corporal Bannister, a lost niece, and a narrow escape. Cissie Vane and Dick's letter also figure in the plot.
76408-willy-s-travels-on-the-railroad:
Mrs. Marcet wrote this book of a boy's trip by rail for young children, printed at London in 1847. The list of parts gives the stops of the trip as small tales. The Railroad stands first, then The Spoiled Child and The Tunnel. Old and Young, the third-class cars with a maid of the mart, and the inn come in the next run. A walk in a park of trees, games of the young, a mill, and a farm fill the mid list.

More tales treat of trees, of the mill from in it, of a great house in the shires, and of the man of the plot. A small coward has two tales, and a small maid who washes has one. The trip ends with a back trip to old friends.
76442-the-dryad:
The Dryad is a novel by Justin Huntly McCarthy, published by Harper and Brothers in 1905. McCarthy also wrote The Proud Prince and Marjorie. A verse dedication sends the pages to the friend who watched the story grow. It calls the tale a legend of the Long Ago, set in the Wonder-Wood where Athenian breezes blow.

Chapter titles name Rainouart, Argathona, and the mystic rose. The Duchess of Thebes, the Catalan Grand Company, and the Knight of Eleusis people the tale. The story retells the Greek past as a romance of gods, knights, and love. Its classical fancy matches the dryad, a wood nymph, of the title.
76667-no-royal-road:
No Royal Road, or the Thing That Lies the Nearest, is a story for girls by Florence Burch. The Sunday School Union published the book in London from Ludgate Hill. This copy is of the thirteenth thousand of the tale in its printing. A frontispiece shows Lilla and her grandmother at the opening of the book.

Contents list twelve chapters for the two girls of the tale in order. Lilla and Margie are introduced, and Lives of Great Women gives them models in the third chapter. A Good Beginning, a new acquaintance, and Lilla awakening Margie ambition follow in the list. The Reward of Diligence, Wasted Minutes, and Which Was the Greatest fill the middle chapters. Burch title states her moral: there is no royal road to a good life, only the nearest duty done well by her girls.
77281-how-to-speak-with-the-dead:
Sciens wrote How to Speak with the Dead, a practical handbook printed in New York in 1918. The author is named only as a writer of standard scientific text-books. Contents open with the question, do the dead still live. Soul and life, telepathy, and mediums follow in order. A chapter on the act of reaching the dead comes next. Working directions fill the seventh chapter, and a last chapter weighs two schools of thought.

The first chapter sets the ground. If life after what is called death is not a fact, the whole idea of speaking with the dead is nonsense. The question is put to religion and to science, and both, the author says, answer yes. All religions teach that a soul parts from the body at death and lives on while the body decays. Such a shared belief, he grants, falls short of proof.
77394-the-druriad:
A satirical poem of 1798, printed for Richardson under the Royal Exchange, takes the performers of Drury Lane Theatre for its subject. Its mottoes are Virgil and Hamlet: use every man after his desert, and who shall escape whipping? The advertisement argues first. Theatres, it says, are instruments by which virtue or vice may be propagated, and everyone, high or low, deems himself a judge of theatrical merit.

That merit is on the wane, and one cause is the laxity of morals pervading ranks. An actor cannot do justice to his part unless he feels the character's energy; debauchery and intoxication impair those powers, if they do not annihilate them. It declares itself blinded by no partiality and stained with no private scandal. Its object is the praise of the meritorious and the ridicule of the undeserving, strictures with notes: the green room judged in verse.
77603-the-hills-of-the-dead:
Robert Howard wrote this tale for Weird Tales, where it ran in August 1930. Solomon Kane, the tall Puritan swordsman, sits by a fire on the Slave Coast with N'Longa, a very old voodoo man and his blood-brother. Finger bones hang at the old man's neck, and the jungle broods black beyond the firelight.

Kane has come back to Africa because the jungle calls him, and with the dawn he goes to seek its heart. N'Longa warns him that those who hear the call may live, but more likely die. Howard builds the tale on atmosphere: red firelight, voodoo talk, and a white wanderer drawn to nameless terror as other men are drawn home.
77761-a-bit-of-rough-road:
A Bit of Rough Road is a religious tale by Amy Le Feuvre, the author of Probable Sons. It was published in London by the Religious Tract Society, with pictures by Percy Tarrant. A line from Gurnall stands at the front. It asks why we complain that heaven's way is rugged, when walking it often will make it smooth.

The chapters follow a girl named Hope. She makes a new friend, faces duties that pull two ways, and makes her choice. Trouble comes, and a new home. One chapter leaves her homeless, with a future unsure. A visit to London and a fruitful search follow. Wedding bells ring before the close. The last chapter is set in a Yorkshire home, by the borderland of the title's road.
77836-the-mystery-road:
The Mystery Road is a novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, published in Boston in 1923. Oppenheim dedicated the story to the memory of Winifred Tolton, his secretary, to whom he had dictated it.

The first chapter shows Myrtile, a French peasant girl, standing on the verandah of a worn white cottage among pine hills. Below her stretch ploughed fields, vines, violets, and an orchard in blossom. She watches three figures come up the path from the village with a look of mute tragedy. The party is led by Jean Sargot, a weather-beaten peasant of the district, with a plump, talkative woman on his arm. Their coming, the reader is told, carries a hidden meaning that Myrtile alone seems to grasp.
77919-sinbad:
Sinbad is a novel by Kay Scott, published in New York by Thomas Seltzer in 1923. The title page calls it a romance. An epigraph from Spinoza's Ethics opens the book, on the nature and force of the emotions and what the mind can do against them.

The contents divide into books named for men. Les fills the first, with chapters called Mirage, Eyes a Year After, and The Ocean. Howard fills the second, through Mirror Maze, The Sleepwalker, and Webs. A third book moves to Algeria, and later books follow other names. The sea captain of the old tales is reworked here into a modern psychological romance. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
78262-giants-bread:
Giants' Bread is a tale of love and doubt by Mary Westmacott, the pen name of Agatha Christie. Its rights were held in nineteen thirty by a great print house. A list of that hand's books stands past the title leaf. A tale left in mid course, a tale of the spring, and a tale of a rose and a yew stand in that list. The book is set in five parts, with a fore tale past them.

The parts of the book bear the names of its folk. A house of great wealth heads the run. Three maids' names own the next three parts. The war and a man of the tale close the list. The fore tale starts on the first night of a new state song house of the great town.
79486-narrative-of-the-surveying-voyages:
Volume two of the narrative of the surveying voyages of the Adventure and Beagle between 1826 and 1836, published at London in 1839. It gives the proceedings of the second expedition, 1831 to 1836, under Captain Robert Fitz-Roy.

The contents open with the Fuegians: their passages across the equator, smallpox, their time in London and at Walthamstow, and their re-embarking. The outfit chapters detail chronometers, boats, lightning-conductors, and the ship's company, Mr Darwin among them. Charts show Tierra del Fuego from the Beagle in 1834 and Chiloé in 1835. The narrative describes the examination of South America's southern shores and the Beagle's circumnavigation of the globe. Naval and science readers get the voyage that carried Darwin, from its captain's pen.
79526-stopping-em-with-lead:
W Wirt fires off a border novelette in Stopping 'Em With Lead, complete in Argosy All-Story Weekly of March 9, 1929. The blurb pairs two lawmen: Jimmie Grant of the Secret Service and Jimmie Earpe, Arizona Ranger. Their alliance starts plenty of trouble for smugglers of dope and for Chinese tong men.

The tale opens on the Benson trail, where a pilot car is waved down with word of Rangers ahead. Driver Mike spins the car onto the alkali, headlights out, doing seventy-five and eighty over the desert. The Kid stands up in the swaying car and empties his Colt at the Border Patrol.
79628-narrative-of-the-surveying-voyages:
Charles Darwin kept a journal of the Beagle's surveying voyage, here as Volume Three. Henry Colburn issued the set in London in 1839. The voyages of the Adventure and Beagle ran from 1826 to 1836. Darwin's part covers his years aboard from 1832 to 1836.

Captain FitzRoy gave up part of his own cabin to house a science man, Darwin writes. Five years of steady kindness from FitzRoy and the officers earn his thanks. Shores of South America and a full circuit of the globe fill the survey. Readers gain the famed journal that first showed Darwin's eye at work.
79700-we-are-the-dead:
We Are the Dead, a tale by Henry Kuttner, appeared in Weird Tales for April 1937, billed as a poignant tale of a weird experience in Arlington Cemetery. Senator Kennicott walks homeward through the cemetery at night after a banquet, grateful for the wind on his flushed face.

Hobson, at his side, will not stop arguing about a bill. Preparedness, Hobson insists, merely protects American interests abroad; the Senator objects that the measure is aggressive and may bring the country closer to war. Hobson hints that the bill will assure the Senator's nomination, and his support is indispensable. Distracted, Kennicott almost walks into a figure standing in darkness beneath a tall elm. A young man, almost a boy, in a faded khaki uniform, his drawn white face full of agony. The boy makes no answer to an apology. Turned away, he says in a muffled tone: I can't sleep.
8078-the-old-homestead:
Mrs Ann S. Stephens, author of Fashion and Famine and many other popular novels, wrote The Old Homestead as a story of New England farm life. Promoted as a superb story of quaint farm life in the vein then popular both in fiction and on the stage. It follows a farm household through the seasons, work, courtship, and family trouble. Stephens was one of America's most prolific storytellers, and her homestead tale aimed at a wide, family audience.

The novel's charm lies in its domestic detail: the house, the fields, and the neighbours who make a farming community. It belongs to the local-colour tradition that celebrated rural New England before the cities drew its young people away. For readers of old American popular fiction, it is a warm, old-fashioned family story.
91-tom-sawyer-abroad:
Tom Sawyer, fresh from river adventures, itches for a wilder trip. Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer Abroad sends Tom, Huck, and Jim aloft in a balloon built by a mad inventor. The craft drifts over the Atlantic toward Africa and the Sahara.

Huck narrates in his own voice as the boys debate geography, fleas, and disappearing lakes. A caravan, a sandstorm, and a treasure hill test Tom's theories. Jim stands siege in one comic set piece after another. The short novel sends Twain's boys beyond the Mississippi for good. Twain's balloon tale satirizes armchair geography while keeping the boys' friendship at its center.
960-the-tin-woodman-of-oz-a-faithful-sto:
L. Frank Baum wrote this faithful story of the Tin Woodman's astonishing adventure, undertaken with Woot the Wanderer, the Scarecrow, and Polychrome, the Rainbow's Daughter. The Tin Woodman, once a woodman turned to tin, sets out with his friends on a quest that tests his heart, such as it is.

Baum follows the party through Oz lands, with humour, magic, and the Tin Woodman's tender care for all living things. Woot's wonder and Polychrome's grace add colour to the road. The book, dedicated to the son of Baum's son Frank, delights Oz readers as a tale of friendship and a heart that proves itself by deeds.
9748-the-old-gray-homestead:
Frances Parkinson Keyes wrote The Old Gray Homestead in 1919, a quiet story of a farm and its folk. Keyes dedicated the book to farmers and their mothers, wives, and daughters, her neighbors and friends of fifteen years. Sally Gray, plain and plump, opens the tale, trading April talk of heat and mud with her brother Austin. The old gray house and its fields anchor the story.

Chapters follow farm work, family talk, and the slow changes of country life, with warmth and exact detail. Keyes writes with love for rural folk, not condescension. A reader gets a gentle farm novel of the postwar years, full of home feeling and the dignity of farm labor.
9865-java-head:
Joseph Hergesheimer's novel takes its name from a Salem shipping house trading with the East, and it opens with young Laurel Ammidon, just turned twelve, weighing the chairs of her childhood home. The Ammidons are a merchant family whose ships and fortunes reach to Java and China.

As Laurel grows, the family's eastern trade brings home people, goods, and ideas that unsettle old Salem ways. Hergesheimer writes in a rich, careful style, attentive to houses, ships, and manners. The novel gives readers a layered portrait of an American port family facing a changing world.
a-man-of-samples-something-about-the-men:
A Man of Samples, by William H Maher, puts a reluctant substitute into a traveling salesman's shoes. Maher opens at midnight. Tom, the regular road man, is off on a wedding tour. The narrator has agreed to take his trip. He is a stock clerk and house salesman of three years. As the hour comes, his courage sinks in proportion.

He tells himself there is nothing to gain. He will not stay on the road. Failure might make his secure place in the house less safe. He eats a heavy hearted supper, bids his landlady and her daughters a solemn goodbye, and goes to the theater to forget. Chapters follow with the road as it was. Hotels, drummers, and orders fat and thin fill them. A sample case introduces him to men across the Midwest.
a-shropshire-lad:
A Shropshire Lad, by A E Housman, collects the short lyrics that made Housman's name, presented here in a 1919 edition with an introduction by William Stanley Braithwaite. Braithwaite praises the poems for wearing reality plainly while turning, in the simplest speech, to sheer loveliness. One English county supplies the ground: cool, tranquil farmland against which brief lives play out.

The lads of the poems soldier, farm, hang, and die young, and the voice speaking for them mixes irony with tenderness. Housman sets happy and painful images side by side without flinching, a habit his introducer calls Grecian in temper. The poems are brief, rhymed, and built to be remembered, which is why lines from them passed into common speech. Readers meet rural England here at its most beautiful and its most fatalistic at once.
a-tramp-abroad:
Mark Twain's travel book recounts a walking tour through Germany and the Alps, and its text notes it was first published in 1880. Twain travels with a companion and reports, in his mock-serious manner, on hotels, porters, river scenery, and the ordeal of learning German. The contents of this first part run from Hamburg and Frankfurt to Heidelberg and its castle.

Set pieces include the legend of the Knave of Bergen, the strange habits of German university students, and their formal duels, described in fascinated detail. Twain also retells Jim Baker's story of blue-jay language, one of his famous tall tales. The humor rests on an American innocent measuring old Europe and finding both wanting and wonderful.
andrew-the-glad: Maria Thompson Daviess writes Andrew the Glad, dedicated to Libbie Luttrell Morrow, with chapters on the heart trap, the ritual, and two little crimes. The novel follows its heroine through Southern society, love, and small misdeeds, with warmth and humour. Daviess gives the story a light, romantic charm typical of her popular fiction.
aunt-jane-s-nieces-abroad:
Edith Van Dyne — L. Frank Baum's pen name for this series — sent the three nieces travelling in this 1906 sequel from Reilly and Britton of Chicago. Beth, Patsy, and Louise tour Europe under Uncle John's wing. The publisher calls them books for girls that older folk also enjoy. Sightseeing fills the road, but real peril waits on it too.

In Sicily, brigands seize a member of the party near Taormina. Uncle John gives the local official a blunt choice. Find his friend at once and return him unharmed. Fail, and soldiers will search the mountains, break up the brigand bands, and disgrace the office that missed them. The official only shrugs, in the expert Sicilian manner. Travel scenes and kidnap drama share the tour from start to finish.
britannica-1911-abbottabad: Abbottabad is the subject of a short town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry sets the town in British India at 4,120 feet, sixty-three miles from Rawalpindi. It heads the Hazara district in the North-West Frontier Province. Sir James Abbott founded it after the Punjab annexation, settling a wild district, and the town bears his name. A brigade headquarters makes it a key military cantonment and hill sanatorium in the northern army corps. Town and cantonment together held 7,764 people in 1901, the entry reports.
britannica-1911-adad:
Adad is the storm-god of the Babylonian-Assyrian pantheon. He is also known as Ramman, the thunderer. The entry admits the double name remains unsolved. Ramman may have been Babylonia's name for him. Adad may have been Assyria's preferred name. Syria's god Hadad is identical with Adad. Aramaic influence likely carried the name into Assyria. Rimmon of Damascus is probably the same god.

Two aspects shape his worship. Rain in due season makes the land fertile. Storms he sends bring havoc and destruction. Monuments picture him with lightning and thunderbolt. Hymns stress his sombre side overall. With the sun-god Shamash he rules divination. Priests invoke both gods over sacrificial livers. Kings call them lords of divination in inscriptions.
britannica-1911-antara-ibn-shaddad:
A long, extravagant romance grew out of ʿAntara ibn Shaddād's life, and his poems travelled for centuries by mouth in the Romance of ʿAntar. Ahlwardt printed the poems at London in 1870; a Beirut edition followed in 1888. The poems themselves braid fighting and love, with Abla as the beloved. His chief poem stands in the Moʿallakát, the famed suspended odes.

ʿAntara was an Arabian poet and warrior of the sixth century. His mother Zabūba was an enslaved African woman; his father Shaddād, a soldier. Neglected in his early years, he won freedom by courage in battle, and his father at last owned him openly. He fought in the war of Dāhis and Ghabrā, a fight between Abs and Dhubyān that began over horses, and he died in battle against the tribe of Ṭai.
britannica-1911-arad:
Arad, a town of Hungary, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of the county of the same name, 159 miles south-east of Budapest by rail. Its people numbered 53,903 in 1900. It stands on the right bank of the river Maros and consists of an inner town and five suburbs. It is a modern-built town with many fine public and private buildings.

The article notes its seats of faith and learning: a Greek Orthodox bishop, a school for his clergy, two schools for training teachers, and a school of music. The town played a large part in the Hungarian rising of 1848 and 1849. A museum holds relics of that war. One square holds a monument to thirteen Hungarian generals shot there in October 1849 on the order of an Austrian general.
britannica-1911-aurangabad:
Aurangabad, a city of India in the lands of the nizam of Hyderabad, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the river Kaum, 138 miles from Poona. It gives its name to a district of 6,172 square miles. The city was founded in 1610 as Fatchnagar by Malik Ambar, an Abyssinian who rose from slavery to great power.

It later became capital of the Mogul conquests in the south of India. Aurangzeb built a tomb for his wife there, compared to the Taj at Agra, and made the city his seat in the Deccan. He gave it its present name. It long stayed capital of the nizams after they broke free of Delhi. When they moved their seat to Hyderabad, the town declined at once. In 1901 its population was 36,837.
britannica-1911-barrhead:
Barrhead, a police burgh in Renfrewshire, Scotland, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a growing town on the Levern, served by the Glasgow and South-Western railway. Its population in 1901 was 9855. Founded in 1773, it had slowly taken in the villages of Arthurlie, Dovecothall, and Grahamston as it grew from a small settlement into a busy working town.

Work in and around Barrhead fills the rest of the entry. Local trades included bleaching, calico-printing, cotton spinning and weaving, iron and brass founding, engineering, and making sanitary fittings. Nearby Neilston had bleachfields and print-works of its own. At Hurlet there were alum and chemical works, while Nitshill, also close by, had chemical works, quarries, and coal mines. Together these places form a small industrial district south-west of Glasgow.
britannica-1911-beachy-head:
Beachy Head is a headland on the Sussex coast of England, south-west of Eastbourne. Its chalk cliff stands 532 feet high, sheer above the sea, and ends the South Downs range to the east. The old Bell Tout lighthouse of 1831 has been replaced by a new light built in the sea at the cliff’s foot.

Much of the entry tells of the naval battle fought here on 30 June 1690, known to the French as Bévisier. A French fleet of over seventy sail under Tourville beat a smaller allied force of English and Dutch ships. Their commander, Torrington, had wanted to fall back and wait for more ships; he was tried for his conduct and cleared.
britannica-1911-bead:
A bead is a small ball or globule used in necklaces. Beads are made of many stuffs: metal, coral, diamond, amber, ivory, stone, clay, glass, rock crystal, and seeds. The word comes from a Middle English term tied to prayer. Beads on a rosary were used to count prayers, and the sense passed from the prayer to the ball itself.

Beads have been made since far-off times and turn up in early tombs in Egypt. Glass beads of many hues, prized in parts of Africa, are thought to be of Egyptian or Phoenician make. Costly beads are strung for wear as ornaments. Cheap kinds trim women's dress. Glass beads have long served as goods for barter. They are made in huge numbers and kinds, above all in Venice, where the craft dates at least to the 1300s.
britannica-1911-berkhampstead:
Berkhampstead, or Great Berkhampstead, is a market town of Hertfordshire, England, twenty-eight miles north-west of London by the London & North-Western railway. It lies in the narrow, well-wooded valley of the Bulbourne, close to the Grand Junction canal. Its urban district counted 5,140 people in 1901.

St Peter’s church, a large cross-shaped building, shows every Gothic style, and the poet William Cowper was born at the rectory in 1731. The grammar school dates from 1541, and straw-plaiting, small wooden wares and chemical works are the trades. The town mattered in Saxon times, with fifty-two burgesses at the Conquest, and rose with its castle under Henry II, who freed its merchants from tolls across his lands.
britannica-1911-birkenhead:
Birkenhead is a seaport borough of Cheshire, England, on the river Mersey. It lies 195 miles north-west of London, directly opposite Liverpool. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 110,915 people in 1901. The town is wholly of modern growth on the Wirral peninsula's east shore. A Benedictine priory was founded there about 1150 by Hamon de Mascy. Its crypt and refectory remains survive, bought for the town in 1896. The priory once lived on Mersey ferry tolls.

Birkenhead grew from a hamlet of some fifty people in 1818. Docks, shipyards, and the ferry trade drove that surge. The article details the great floating dock basins and graving docks at length. One graving dock runs about 900 feet long and 130 feet wide. The borough became a parliamentary borough in 1861 and gained a municipal charter in 1877. Tranmere, Claughton, and Oxton suburbs fall inside its bounds.
britannica-1911-bridge-head:
Bridge-head, from the French tete-du-pont, names the field works that guard an army's crossing of a river. Guns and defences are set on one bank or both so troops can pass over bridges without hostile meddling. Because moving an army across is slow and tangled, the guard works must sit far enough out to keep enemy cannon beyond range of the bridges.

Space matters as much as safety: troops need room to form up on the far bank once across. In earlier days, when weapons reached only a short way, a bridge-head could be little more than a screen for the bridge itself. Modern arms changed that scale, forcing bridge defences to stretch much farther out, a shift the short entry stresses as its main point.
britannica-1911-bursian-conrad:
Conrad Bursian, a German scholar of the old tongues and of old remains, born in eighteen thirty, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Mutzschen in Saxony, he moved with his kin to Leipzig as a boy. He was schooled there and went to the town high school in eighteen forty seven. He studied under two famed men of the craft.

He spent six months in Berlin to hear a great teacher there. He then closed his school years back at Leipzig. The next three years went to roads through Belgium, France, Italy, and Greece. He rose step by step as a teacher in town after town. Chairs at four towns mark the climb. His last chair was at Munich, where he stayed till his death in eighteen eighty three. The entry traces a full map of the German school world of his age.
britannica-1911-carlsbad:
Carlsbad is a celebrated watering-place of Bohemia, in Austria. Its Czech name is Karlovy Vary. It lies 116 miles west-north-west of Prague by rail. Its population in 1900 was 14,640. This long 1911 Britannica article describes the spa town. It stands at an altitude of 1227 feet. It fills the narrow, winding valley of the Tepl. Granite hills covered with pine forest hem it in.

The houses climb the mountain sides in tiers of terraces. Long flights of steps and steep roads reach them. The Catholic parish church dates from 1732–1736, in rococo style. A gorgeous Russian church was finished in 1897. The Mühlbrunnen Colonnade is the town's famous building. It was erected between 1871 and 1878. Its 103 granite Corinthian columns line the promenade. The Kurhaus and the Kaiserbad serve the bathers. The Sprudel Colonnade shelters the great hot spring.
britannica-1911-chad:
Chad is a lake of northern Central Africa, described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It lies about eight hundred fifty feet above the sea. It sits in a borderland between the fertile wooded Sudan to the south and dry steppes that merge into the Sahara to the north.

The lake area is shrinking as the country dries, the entry says. That drying has been fairly fast since the middle of the last century. A town on its south shore in eighteen fifty was over twenty miles from the water by nineteen oh five. The west shore is flat, so a slight rise floods a large area. That fact skews estimates of the lake's size. Sand hills ring the north shores, and the east shows the drying most.
britannica-1911-corn-salad:
Corn salad, also called lamb lettuce, is a weedy plant grown for salads. Its plant entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is native to southern Europe and now grows wild in cornfields. In France it serves in winter and spring in place of lettuce.

Growers raise the plant from seed sown on light rich earth beds. Beds need weed and water care till winter cold sets in. Long litter guards the crop when hard frost strikes the beds late. The largest plants are drawn first for use in a steady order. Sowing can run each two or three weeks from August to October.
britannica-1911-el-wad:
El Wad is a town in the Algerian Sahara, south east of Biskra. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Counts from nineteen o six put its people at just over seven thousand. Huge hollows with noble palm groves ring the town on all sides.

Past those groves the endless desert spreads with great waves of sand. Ceaseless toil alone holds that sand back from the oasis fields. The town is a mass of one floor stone houses with domes. They cluster round the market place with its mosque and tall minaret. No walls guard the town save a French fort on the south.
britannica-1911-elisavetgrad:
Elisavetgrad is covered in a short hosted fragment that opens mid-entry, starting with the population figure of 66,182 in 1900. The fragment describes a regularly built town with wide streets, some of them lined with trees. It calls the place a wealthy town and an industrial centre for its region. No opening lines naming the town's setting survive in the hosted text.

Its steam flour-mills rank second only to Odessa, and its works include distilleries, mechanical workshops, tobacco and tallow factories, and brickworks. The town trades in cereals and flour for export, and in sheep, cattle, wool, leather, and timber, with five fairs held each year. The fragment also notes a military school, a first-class weather station, and a botanical garden. The town was founded in 1754 and named after the empress Elizabeth, and its fortifications are now decayed.
britannica-1911-flamborough-head:
Flamborough Head is a promontory on the Yorkshire coast of England, between the Filey and Bridlington bays of the North Sea. It is a lofty chalk headland. Its power to resist the waves shows clearly against the low coast of Holderness to the south, which the sea eats away. Yet the cliffs of the Head are pierced with caverns and fringed with rocks of fantastic outline, worn into strange shapes by the water.

Remarkable twisting of the chalk strata can be seen at various points along the cliffs. Sea-birds breed in plenty on their ledges, out of reach of most predators. A lighthouse marks the point, at latitude 54 degrees 7 minutes north and longitude 0 degrees 5 minutes west. The entry is short, giving the headland's place, its chalk, its caves and birds, and the light that warns ships off it.
britannica-1911-fredrikstad:
Fredrikstad is a seaport and manufacturing town of Norway in Smaalenene county, 58 miles south of Christiania on the Christiania-Gothenburg railway. It lies at the mouth of Christiania fjord on both banks of the Glommen river, which floats down great rafts of timber from the wooded Österdal district. Its population in 1900 was 14,553.

The new town on the right bank is the chief Norwegian port for pit-props, planed boards, and other timber, and red bricks are made in quantity for the growing cities nearby. Granite quarrying, saw and planing mills, shipbuilding yards, and cotton and woollen mills fill out the industry. An ice-breaker keeps the harbour open in winter. The old town on the left bank was founded by Frederick II in 1567 and long fortified; Charles XII tried and failed to take it in 1716.
britannica-1911-fyzabad:
Fyzabad, or Faizabad, is a city of the United Provinces in British India, standing on the left bank of the Gogra 78 miles by rail east of Lucknow. Its population in 1901 was 75,085, and the ancient site of Ajodhya adjoins it as a suburb. The city was founded about 1730 by Saadat Ali Khan, the first nawab wazir of Oudh, who built a hunting-lodge there. Shuja-ud-daula, the third nawab, laid out a large town, fortified it and was buried there.

When the court of Oudh moved to Lucknow in 1775, the merchants and bankers left, and by 1869 the population had fallen to 37,804. In the Mutiny of 1857 the native garrison rose, and of the Europeans escaping by boat toward Dinapur, nearly all were lost. The district of Fyzabad, between the Gogra and the Gumti, covers 1740 square miles and held 1,225,374 people in 1901. Sugar-refining and trade in farm produce are its chief industries.
britannica-1911-gad:
Gad, in the Bible, names a prophet and a tribe of Israel. The prophet Gad was a seer who kept company with David. He warned David to take refuge in Judah and announced God's anger at the numbering of the people. Later tradition joined him with Nathan in ordering the music and credited him with an account of David's deeds. The tribe traced its descent from Jacob's son by Zilpah, Leah's maid.

The name is that of a god of fortune. The tribe's fortunes were bound up with Reuben's, and its towns are placed now south, now north of Heshbon. Mesha's inscription, from about 850 B.C., speaks of Gad holding Ataroth east of the Dead Sea. Later the tribe sat in Gilead, a district open to raiders. Its men had a name for bravery, and its history runs with the northern kingdom until 734 B.C.
britannica-1911-gateshead:
Gateshead is a borough of Durham, England, on the south bank of the Tyne facing Newcastle. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its population as 109,888 in 1901. Three bridges link it to Newcastle, and its parish church of St Mary is an old cruciform building with a tall tower. A fire in 1854 destroyed much of the town.

Its works are heavy: iron foundries, engine and boiler factories, shipbuilding yards, glass, chemical and soap works, and a big railway depot. Coal mines lie nearby, and the grindstone quarries of Gateshead Fell are exported worldwide, the entry says. The long history section runs from Bishop Walcher's murder there in 1080 through centuries under the bishops of Durham. It records trade fights with Newcastle and notes the town had no member of parliament until 1832.
britannica-1911-ghaziabad: Ghaziabad is a town of British India in the Meerut district of the United Provinces. It lies twelve miles from Delhi and twenty eight miles from Meerut. Its people numbered eleven thousand two hundred seventy five in nineteen o one. The town was founded in seventeen forty by Ghazi ud din, and takes its name from him. He was a son of the first nizam of the Deccan. Ghaziabad has grown as a rail junction, where three rail systems meet. The town trades in grain and hides.
britannica-1911-gold-and-silver-thread:
Gold and Silver Thread, in the 1911 Britannica, covers gold and silver strips, threads and gimp used in weaving, embroidery, twisting, plaiting and lace work. The entry opens with the living craft: in many oriental centres, it says, early traditions of such fabrics survive, and the taste for them stays strong.

The history runs deep. Aaron's ephod in Exodus, beaten gold cut into wires and worked into coloured linen, is the first exhibit. Homer's poems, Assyrian sculpture of King Assur-nasir-pal's robe, and Persian splendour under Darius follow. Pliny credits Attalus of Pergamum with inventing weaving with gold, giving the Attalic cloths. Roman dress, the tunics of Agrippina and Heliogabalus, and the craft's later course fill the long article. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the thread article stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-goliad:
Goliad, a village in Texas and the seat of Goliad county, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the north bank of the San Antonio river, eighty five miles south east of San Antonio. The entry gives it about 1,700 people in 1900. Rich farming and stock land surrounds it, and it has flour mills, cotton gins, and cotton seed oil mills.

Here stand the ruins of the old Spanish mission of La Bahia, moved to this spot in 1747. The name Goliad, first used about 1829, is likely an anagram of Hidalgo, the Mexican patriot. On the outbreak of the Texan war, a small Mexican garrison here surrendered in October 1835. A first declaration of independence was issued at Goliad that December. In 1836 Colonel Fannin held the town with about 350 Americans.
britannica-1911-hadad:
Hadad was the name of a Syrian deity. The name also appears in the Old Testament for several men. Compound forms include Benhadad and Hadadezer. The god behind the name is a storm-god. He was also known as Ramman, Bir and Dadda. Kings of Damascus habitually took the title Benhadad. That means son of Hadad. Egyptian kings likewise called themselves sons of Amon-Ra.

Much of the discussion turns on one phrase in Zechariah. It speaks of the mourning of Hadadrimmon in Megiddo's valley. Jerome and older interpreters read a place name there. They tied the mourning to Josiah's death. Newer opinion reads Hadadrimmon as another name for Adonis. The mourning would then be the Adonis festival laments. Cheyne argued the Septuagint's simple Rimmon supports some corruption. His rendering gives women weeping for Tammuz-Adon.
britannica-1911-halmstad:
Halmstad is a Swedish seaport on the Cattegat. It is chief town of the district of Halland. Gothenburg lies 76 miles to the north-west by rail. The population in 1900 was 15,362. The town stands at the mouth of the river Nissa. It has an inner harbour, an outer harbour and open roads. Granite quarries nearby export stone chiefly to Germany. Engineering, shipbuilding and brewing employ many.

Cloth, jute, hats, wood-pulp and paper are also made. Exports run to granite, timber and hats. Salmon fisheries in the district are valuable. The town's church is mentioned as early as 1462. Its oldest privileges date from 1307. Under the Kalmar union it was chosen for electing Scandinavian kings. Gustavus Vasa took it from the Danes in 1534. The treaty of Copenhagen ceded it to Sweden in 1660. Charles XII beat a Danish army nearby in 1676.
britannica-1911-henke-heinrich-philipp-k:
Heinrich Philipp Konrad Henke (1752–1809) was a German theologian. He was born at Hehlen in Brunswick on 3 July 1752. Brunswick's gymnasium and Helmstädt university educated him. From 1778 to 1809 he professed at Helmstädt. Philosophy came first, then theology, in his chairs. In 1803 he also became principal of Brunswick's Carolinum. He died on 2 May 1809. He belonged to the rationalistic school of theology.

His principal work is a general history of the Christian church. It ran to six volumes between 1788 and 1804. Baur commended its fullness, accuracy and artistic composition. His Lineamenta of 1783 presented historical-critical theology. Sermons and academic opuscula are also listed. He edited journals on religion, philosophy and church history. His son Ernst Ludwig Theodor Henke became a Marburg professor. The son wrote monographs on Calixt and Pius VII. Church history thus ran in the family.
britannica-1911-hogshead:
A hogshead is a cask for holding liquor or goods such as tobacco, sugar and molasses. It is also a measure of capacity, and the measure varies with the contents. For beer and cider it equals 54 gallons. A statute of Richard III in 1483 fixed the hogshead of wine at 63 wine-gallons, that is, 52½ imperial gallons.

The word's origin has been much discussed. Skeat finds it in a Teutonic name for a cask found in Dutch, Danish and Old Swedish forms like oxhooft and oxehoved. On that view the true word is oxhead, and hogshead is a corruption, perhaps from branding the measure with an ox's head. The New English Dictionary takes the opposite line: it makes hogshead the original form, from which the other languages' forms were corrupted. Earlier Dutch forms hukeshovet and hoekshoot stand nearer the English, and the Dutch for ox is os.
britannica-1911-holyhead:
Holyhead, in Welsh Caergybi, is a seaport and market town of Anglesey, North Wales, on the small Holy Island at the county's western end. Its urban district held 10,079 people in 1901. The London and North-Western railway ends here, 263½ m. from London. An embankment three-quarters of a mile long joins Holy Island to Anglesey, carrying road and rail over fast tides.

Once a small fishing village, Holyhead grew from William IV's reign as the Dublin mail steam station. Its great harbour of refuge was begun in 1847 and opened in September 1873. The north breakwater runs 7,860 ft., and roadstead and enclosed water together give fine shelter. The works cost the railway company nearly a million and a half pounds, the rubble mound being swept away by storms again and again. Later quay works were opened by the prince of Wales in 1880.
