George IV passed through in 1821 on his way to Ireland.
britannica-1911-jacobabad: Jacobabad, a town of British India, is noted in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It serves as the head town of the Upper Sind frontier district in Bombay. It is famed for having the highest heat in India on a steady basis. In June the scale ranges far above one hundred degrees. The town was founded in eighteen forty seven by General John Jacob, on the site of a village. Cavalry barracks and caravan lodging stand there, and two canals water the town.
britannica-1911-jihad:
Jihad is an Arabic word whose plain sense is an effort or a contest, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains its use as a duty in Islam. It names the duty laid down in the Koran for the followers of Mahomet to make war on those who reject the faith. That duty appears in five suras, all from the time after Mahomet had gained power.

Muslim scholars, the entry notes, do not read these commands as a standing order for all believers to war on unbelievers at all times. A general war, it is held, can be called only by the caliph, an office then claimed by the sultans of Turkey. Groups that reject the sultan's lead, such as the Persians and Moors, look to their own rulers for such a call.
britannica-1911-khalil-ibn-ahmad:
Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, an Arabian philologist who lived from 718 to 791, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. A native of Oman, he was distinguished for writing the first Arabic dictionary. He also first classified the Arabic metres and laid down their rules. He was a poet as well. He lived the ascetic life of a poor student.

Khalīl's grammatical work was carried on by his pupil Sībawaihī. The dictionary known as the Kitāb-ul-ʿAin is ascribed to him, at least in its start. A pupil probably finished it. Its words are not in alphabetical order but follow a scheme based on the organs of speech. The work is now known only from extracts. Other grammatical works bear his name, though their authenticity is doubted.
britannica-1911-kokstad:
Kokstad is a town of South Africa, the capital of Griqualand East. It lies 236 miles by rail S.W. of Durban. It is also 110 miles N. by W. of Port Shepstone, and 150 miles N. of Port St John in Pondoland. In 1904 it held 2903 people, a third of them Griquas. The town stands on the outer slopes of the Drakensberg, 4270 feet above the sea. Mount Currie rises behind it to 7297 feet, and a fine water supply comes from the mountains.

Well laid out, with several handsome public buildings, Kokstad is the centre of a rich farming district. It trades in wool, grain, cattle and horses with Basutoland, Pondoland and the nearby parts of Natal. The town is named for the Griqua chief Adam Kok, who founded it in 1869. It passed to Cape Colony in 1879, gained municipal government in 1893, and is the home of the Headman of the Griqua nation.
britannica-1911-kristianstad:
Kristianstad is a port of Sweden and chief town of the district of the same name. It stands on a peninsula in Lake Sjövik, a widening of the river Helge, 10 miles from the Baltic. In 1900 it held 10,318 people. Its harbour and custom-house lie at Åhus, at the river mouth. The town ranks among the first twelve in Sweden for the value of its manufactures, which include engineering works, flour-mills, distilleries, weaving mills and sugar factories. The hosted text is one segment of a shared file holding neighbouring entries.

Granite and wood-pulp go out, and coal and grain come in. The town is the seat of the court of appeal for the provinces of Skane and Blekinge. Christian IV of Denmark founded and fortified it in 1614. The town passed to Sweden in 1658, was retaken by Christian V in 1676, and was won by Sweden again in 1678.
britannica-1911-kroonstad:
Kroonstad is a town of the Orange River Colony, 127 miles by rail N.E. of Bloemfontein and 130 miles S.W. of Johannesburg. In 1904 it held 7191 people, of whom 3708 were whites. It stands 4489 feet above the sea, on the banks of the Valsch River. The town is the centre of a rich farming district and of the diamond and coal work of the north-west of the colony. Its healthy climate draws visitors from Johannesburg.

When the British took Bloemfontein in the Anglo-Boer War, the Boers made Kroonstad their capital, from the 13th of March to the 11th of May 1900. Lord Roberts occupied it the next day. A link made in 1906 gave the town the shortest rail route between Cape Town and Durban.
britannica-1911-kuruntwad:
Kuruntwad, or Kurandvad, is a native state of India, in the Deccan division of Bombay. It forms part of the Southern Mahratta jagirs. The state was first made in 1772 by a grant from the peshwa. In 1811 it was split into two parts, one of which, Shedbal, lapsed to the British in 1857. In 1855 Kuruntwad was split again, between a senior and a junior branch. The lands of both branches lie scattered among other states and British districts.

The senior branch covers 185 square miles, held 42,474 people in 1901, and has a revenue of £13,000. The junior branch covers 114 square miles, held 34,003 people, and has £9000. Their joint tribute is £640. The chiefs are Brahmans of the Patwardhan family. The town of Kuruntwad, where both branches live, stands on the right bank of the Panchganga river, near its meeting with the Kistna, and held 10,451 people in 1901.
britannica-1911-lanterns-of-the-dead: Lanterns of the Dead are small stone towers in the centre and west of France. Small openings near the top held a light at night. The light marked the place of a graveyard. Most towers are round. A low door and a pulley served the lamp. The Cellefrouin tower is held the finest in France. Eight joined half-round shafts form it. One opening faces the main road.
britannica-1911-lead:
Lead is a metallic element known since the earliest ages. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with its ancient uses. Its sign Pb comes from the Latin word plumbum. Scripture names the metal, and Romans used it for water pipes.

Roman plumbers joined those pipes with a lead and tin mix. Pliny wrote of black lead and white lead as two kinds. White lead was known to writers by the eighth century. Alchemists marked the metal with the sign of Saturn. Pure lead is rare in nature and found in small amounts. Its chief ore is galena, which spreads across the world. That ore always carries some silver locked inside it. English mines in Derbyshire lead the home list in the entry.
britannica-1911-marblehead:
Marblehead is a township in Essex County in Massachusetts, set on a rocky point on the bay north of Boston. The entry gives its size and counts of folk at past counts. Old houses from the two past centuries line its streets. The Lee house, an old church, and the old town hall are named as sights.

The town tale takes up much of the piece. Settlers came about sixteen twenty-nine, and the town was set up on its own in sixteen forty-nine. It was a busy port in colonial days. The text tells of its ships and men in the war for freedom, and of shoe making and yachts in later years.
britannica-1911-marienbad:
Marienbad is a spa town in Bohemia, then part of Austria. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its springs and cure. It lies west of Prague on the edge of a great forest. Pine clad hills ring it on all sides but the south.

Eight mineral springs belong to the abbey of Tepl nearby. Guests both bathe in and drink the waters. Some springs carry salts like those of Carlsbad, but cold. Others rank among the strongest iron waters in the world. Doctors sent liver, gout, and weight cases to take the cure. A strict diet ruled the guest stay at the spa. Moor mud baths used peat rich in iron. A million bottles of the water shipped out each year.
britannica-1911-moorhead:
Moorhead, a city in Clay County, Minnesota, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat, set on the east bank of the Red River. Fargo, in North Dakota, faces it across the water. The census of 1910 counted 4,840 people there.

Two rail lines, the Great Northern and the Northern Pacific, served the city. Moorhead holds one of the state normal schools, founded in 1888. Concordia College, a Norwegian Lutheran school of 1891, had five hundred students a few years before the article. The city was named in honour of James Moorhead, a Pennsylvania congressman of the Civil War years. It was settled in 1871, made a village in 1875, and chartered as a city in 1881. The short article gives the place as a rail and schooling centre for its farm district.
britannica-1911-moradabad:
Moradabad is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a city and district of British India in the United Provinces. The city stands on the right bank of the Ramganga river, 655 feet above the sea and 868 miles by rail from Calcutta, with 75,128 people in 1901. Rustam Khan founded it in 1625 and built the fort above the river bank and the great Jama Masjid mosque of 1631. The town forms a large centre of trade in country produce.

Its special craft is ornamental brassware, sometimes plated with lac or tin and then engraved, and cotton weaving and printing are also carried on. The district, 2,285 square miles of the great Gangetic plain east of the Ganges, is cut into three parts by the Ramganga and the Sot rivers.
britannica-1911-murshidabad:
Murshidabad is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town and district in Bengal, in British India. The town stands on the left bank of the Bhagirathi, an old channel of the Ganges. Its count in 1901 was 15,168 people.

The article calls the town the last Muslim capital of Bengal. In 1704 the nawab moved his seat there from Dacca and gave it his own name. Great banking houses kept their posts there for many years. The text tours palaces, mosques, tombs, and gardens, and names work in ivory, gold thread, silk, and silver thread. It then sketches the wider district, split in two by the river.
britannica-1911-nagy-varad:
Nagy-Varad, in German Grosswardein, a town of Hungary, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of the county of Bihar, 153 miles east south east of Budapest by rail. The entry gives it 47,018 people in 1900. It stands in a plain on both banks of the river Sebeskoros.

The town is the seat of a Roman Catholic bishop and of a Greek bishop as well. Its chief buildings include the church of Saint Ladislaus, built in 1723, which holds the remains of that king. A Roman Catholic cathedral, a Greek cathedral, and a large rococo bishop's palace also stand there. Schools include a law academy, a seminary, and gymnasiums of two faiths. The town is a key railway junction with brisk trade in farm produce, cattle, horses, fruit, and wine. Warm baths lie six miles south.
britannica-1911-nomad: Nomad is a word for one who roams, from Greek terms for one who roams in search of grass for beasts. It is used most for tribes that shift from place to place to feed their herds. In Greek books of old the word named most of all the herds folk of North Africa. From that use came the Latin name for the Numidian folk. The entry is a brief note that gives just the root and the chief old use.
britannica-1911-pad:
Pad is a word with several distinct senses, set out in this 1911 Britannica article on its origins and uses. The first sense links it with pod, a husk or seed case, and with the idea of a soft cushion used for cover or stuffing. In the study of animals it names the fleshy pads on the sole of the foot of cats, dogs, and camels.

In sport, the whole paw of a fox or other hunted beast is called the pad. A second old sense, from a word for path or track, survives in footpad, a highway robber, and pad horse, an easy going road horse. A third sense is a dialect word for a frog or toad, better known in its small form, paddock.
britannica-1911-pellicanus-conrad:
Pellicanus, Conrad is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a German church scholar of the Reformation age. Conrad Pellicanus was born at Ruffach in Alsace on the eighth of January 1478 and died in 1556. His German name, Kursner, was changed to the Latin Pellicanus by his uncle, a churchman linked to the university of Heidelberg, who backed his studies there.

Back home, the young man taught without pay in a friars' school so that he could borrow books from its store. At sixteen he chose to become a friar himself, a step that sent him to Tubingen in 1496 and brought him under a learned guardian of the house there. The article stresses how slow and calm his move toward Protestant views was, with none of the sharp break that marked Luther. It paints a bookish life shaped by hunger for learning in three tongues.
britannica-1911-peterhead:
Peterhead is a burgh and seaport of Aberdeenshire, the most easterly town in Scotland. Its people numbered eleven thousand seven hundred ninety four in nineteen o one. It stands about thirty three miles by road from Aberdeen. The town is built of the red granite for which it is famed. Quarrying that stone, for home and foreign use, is a chief trade there.

Chief buildings include the town house of seventeen eighty eight, with a spire one hundred twenty five feet high. An art gallery and museum also stand in the town. A statue of Field Marshal Keith stands before the town hall. Peterhead once traded much with ports of the Baltic and America. For a long period it was the chief seat of the Greenland trade. Its seal and whale fishery is now extinct, the entry says.
britannica-1911-peutinger-konrad:
Konrad Peutinger (1465–1547) was a German humanist and student of old things, born at Augsburg. In 1497 he became town clerk of his home city. He was on close terms with the emperor Maximilian. He was one of the first men to print Roman stone inscriptions. His name stays tied to the famed Tabula Peutingeriana, a map of the war roads of the western Roman Empire.

Konrad Celtes found that map and passed it to Peutinger to print. Peutinger also edited the Historia Gothorum of Jordanes and the history of the Lombards by Paulus Diaconus. The map was first printed as a whole by F. de Scheyb in 1753. Later editions came from Desjardins and from Miller in the late 19th century. The article closes with a short list of works on the map and its meaning.
britannica-1911-pleiad: Pleiad, a name for a set of seven poets, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In Greek literature the Alexandrian critics gave the name to seven tragic poets of the reign of Ptolemy Philadelphus. In French literature there were two famed groups of the kind. The first, under Henri the Third, was led by Pierre de Ronsard and sought to raise French letters by copying the classics. The second, under Louis the Thirteenth, was made of authors skilled in Latin verse.
britannica-1911-roundhead:
Roundhead is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name was used for the men who backed Parliament in the English Civil War. It came from the short hair worn by some Puritans, cut close round the head. That plain style stood out next to the long curls worn by men of fashion.

The article traces the first uses of the word as a term of scorn in late 1641. It cites a crowd at Westminster, an officer named David Hide, and Clarendon's History of the Rebellion. A rival tale links the word to a remark by Queen Henrietta Maria at the trial of Strafford. The piece also notes how Roundhead and Cavalier soon formed a matched pair in common speech.
britannica-1911-shad:
Shad is the name given to certain wandering species of herring, and a natural history entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica picks out their marks. Shad differ from the true herrings by a plain trait. They have no teeth at all in the jaws. Two species occur in Europe, and they look much alike.

One is the allis shad, and the other is the twaite shad. Both are greenish on the back and silvery on the sides, like most herrings. A large blackish blotch behind the gill opening marks them out. A row of like spots runs along the middle of the side behind that blotch. The two kinds are so closely allied that their separateness is hard to prove. The entry gives anglers and naturalists a guide to a prized food fish.
britannica-1911-sheepshead:
Sheepshead is one of the largest fish of its genus, described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Its kin are sea fish known on the coasts of south Europe. The fish has two kinds of teeth. Flat teeth like front teeth sit in a row at the front of the jaws.

Round teeth like molars sit in rows at the sides of the jaws. The fish is found in plenty on the Atlantic coast of the United States. It runs from Cape Cod to Florida, and is a prized food fish. It may reach thirty inches long, the entry says. It feeds on shellfish, which it tears from their base and crushes. Dark bands cross its body. The same name is given in places to a fresh water fish held in lower regard.
britannica-1911-spurn-head:
Spurn Head, also called Spurn Point, is a narrow spit of land on the coast of Yorkshire in England. A short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica fixes its place at the mouth of the Humber. It runs near four miles from the village of Kilnsea. Yet it is seldom more than three hundred yards wide, and it rises only a few feet above the sea.

The spit is made of sand and shingle swept down from the soft coast of Holderness. Currents drag some six million tons of that coast away each year. Deep water lies close off the sea side of the head. The spit seems to have formed in fairly late times, since about 1600. Two lighthouses and a lifeboat station stand on it.
britannica-1911-sweetbread: Sweetbread is a common name for set glands of animals when they are used as food, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Most often it means the pancreas, which butchers call the stomach sweetbread. It can also mean the thymus, called the breast sweetbread. At times the term takes in the salivary glands and the lymph glands as well. The entry sends readers to the texts on ductless glands, the pancreas, and the lymphatic system for the full account of each part and its work in the body.
britannica-1911-timgad:
Timgad, a ruined city in Algeria, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies south-east of Batna in the district of Constantine. The Romans knew it as Thamugas, and built it on the low slopes of the Aures Mountains. Six roads met at the spot where the town was laid out.

Two main streets crossed the town, one north and south, one east and west. The homes of the town lay lower than its public buildings. The capitol held a proud place in the south-west of the city. Some of its tall columns, of the Corinthian order, have been set up anew. Its size is the same as that of the Pantheon at Rome, the entry notes. The piece goes on to walk the reader through the chief ruins.
britannica-1911-toad:
Toad is the folk name for stout frogs with warty skin in this beast entry in the 1911 Britannica. Shape alone is a poor guide, since some slim kinds out leap true frogs. The true toad stock bears no teeth in its jaws at all. Its chief kind is the common toad found through the home isles. Near a hundred kinds of that stock range the world save two far lands.

Two kinds live in the British Isles by the count of the text. The natterjack runs on short legs and seldoms hops at all. Its male bears a throat pouch that blows past the size of its head. Toads lay their eggs in long strings of clear jelly tubes. One small kind in east Africa bears its young alive, a lone case known.
britannica-1911-trinidad:
Trinidad is an island article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It presents Trinidad as the most southerly of the British West Indian islands. The island lies just east of the coast of Venezuela. The entry gives its length, breadth, and area, and notes its almost square shape.

Inside, the article describes the land in detail. Two ranges of forested hills run along the north and south. The entry names the Maracas Falls, which drop over a sheer wall of rock. It gives long space to the Pitch Lake at La Brea, a wide pool of natural asphalt. The lake was worked by a company that shipped the asphalt to the United States. Readers get a full picture of the island's ground, waters, and chief natural wonders.
britannica-1911-troy-and-troad:
Troy and Troad deals with the land of Troy, the north west point of Asia Minor. Homer never uses the name Troad, but later Greek writers do. Seas bound the land on the north, west, and south. The range of Ida forms its east edge and shapes the whole tract.

The entry first fixes those bounds with care, since old writers drew them in unlike ways. Ida is called the key to the lay of the land. The chief river, the Scamander, rises in Ida and drains the core plain. That plain splits in two parts, and the text maps each part in turn.
britannica-1911-woad: Woad is a herb plant known in botany as Isatis tinctoria, of the cabbage order. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes an upright branched stem one to three feet high. Sessile leaves and clusters of small yellow flowers mark the plant. Its brown hanging pods run about two inches long. The plant grows here and there in England in fields and chalk pits. Ancient Britons stained their bodies with it, the entry recalls. It was still grown for use in Lincolnshire at that time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-woodh:
Abraham Woodhead was a voluminous controversial writer born at Almonbury, Yorkshire, about March 1609. He died at Hoxton, Middlesex, on 4 May 1678. Educated at University College, Oxford, he entered in 1624, fellow from 1633 and proctor from 1641. He began, while travelling abroad in 1645, thinking of joining the Catholic Church. Ejected from his fellowship in 1648, he tutored the young Duke of Buckingham and lived with friends until 1654.

In 1654 he and other Catholics bought a house at Hoxton for a community life of devotion and study. Restored to his fellowship in 1660, he soon returned to Hoxton, where he lived on its income until his death, busy with literary labour. His chief works were Ancient Church Government, Guide in Controversies, and four works against Stillingfleet. He also translated St. Teresa's life and St. Augustine's Confessions, and his manuscripts passed to Sir Thomas Brooke's collection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-allahabad:
Allahabad is a diocese suffragan to Agra in India, between 28 and 30 degrees north and 77 and 88 degrees east. It covers 150,000 square miles. It sits between Calcutta and Agra east and west, and between Bettiah, the Himalayas, and Nagpur north and south. The mission dates from 1669. Matheus de Castro, a Goan Indian and a Brahmin by caste, was charged by Propaganda with the kingdom of the Great Mogul.

The field proved too vast and the labourers too few. In 1703 Propaganda erected the Prefecture of Tibet and adjoining countries for the Ancona Capuchins. The diocese counts 8,800 Catholics out of 38,174,000 people, mostly Mussulmans and Hindus. Benares, the sacred Hindu city and centre of their religious activity, sits within the diocese. The mission counts 22 Capuchins, 3 secular priests, 18 Christian Brothers, and 74 nuns of the Institute of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Six orphanages hold about 450 children, and educational establishments teach 1,468 pupils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arad: Arad was a titular see in Palestine, said to match the hill of Tell Arad on the road from Petra to Hebron, named in Numbers 21:1 and Judges 1:16. Its bishops' list is given in Le Quien's Oriens Christianus, with Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography cited as a further source. The entry is a bare gazetteer note, fixing a biblical place to a former bishop's seat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bagdad:
Bagdad was founded on the Tigris by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur in 762 or 764. He named it Medinet es-Selam, City of Salvation, while Bagdad is said to mean Garden of Dat. For five centuries it served as the rich, brilliant capital of the Arabian Empire. Hulagu, grandson of Genghis Khan, entered it in 1262, and it passed to Kara Koyunlu Turks, then to Tamerlane.

Persians took it in 1517 and ruled, save a short break, until Sultan Murad made it Ottoman in 1638. It remains the chief town of its vilayet, and the most important city of Asiatic Turkey after Damascus and Smyrna. It exports textiles, gold and silverware, horses, and dates, and holds many beautiful mosques and old wall ruins. Its climate is hot, fevers are frequent, and plague sometimes appears, while its population figures are shaky at best.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-csanad:
A diocesan entry covers Csanad, a Hungarian see suffragan to Kalocsa, spanning 13,713 square miles with over two million people, of whom 824,000 were Catholics. It lists a cathedral chapter, 236 parish churches, 1,099 filial churches, and hundreds of clergy, plus male orders and sisters' convents across the diocese.

One of Hungary's oldest sees, Csanad was founded by King Stephen in 1035, its first bishop the Italian abbot Gerard, tutor to Stephen's son. Mongol invasion in the thirteenth century, Serb immigration in the fourteenth, and later Turkish pressure battered it repeatedly. Its baroque cathedral at Temesvar, built 1736 to 1754, is dedicated to St. George, and a seminary for boys rose under Bishop Bonnaz between 1860 and 1889.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gad:
Gad is one name worn by four figures in the Bible: a patriarch, a tribe, a prophet, and a pagan god of fortune. The patriarch was Jacob's seventh son and first by Zilpah, Leah's maid, born in Mesopotamia. At his birth Leah cried Happily, and the name Gad keeps that cry. Scripture names his seven sons and says no more of him himself.

The tribe of Gad settled east of the Jordan, between Manasseh to the north and Reuben to the south, on land prized for herds. Over 40,000 strong in the desert march, the Gadites crossed to help conquer western Palestine, then held the east bank for centuries as its chief Israelite tribe. Warlike and praised in Moses' blessing, they guarded a frontier whose borders shifted with the ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lead:
Lead is a South Dakota diocese erected 6 August 1902, covering all the state west of the Missouri River, 41,759 square miles, with the bishop's residence at Hot Springs. Its ground came from Nebraska's vicariate apostolic, holding about 6,000 Catholics in 1902, including Sioux reservation Indians.

First bishop John Stariha, vicar-general of St. Paul, was consecrated there on 28 October 1902. Born in Carniola in 1845, he had long pastored St. Francis de Sales in St. Paul. Opening the Rosebud Reservation and new railways drew settlers, parishes, churches, missions, and Indian schools. Ill health made him resign in 1909 and return to Austria, and Pius X ratified Joseph Busch of Excelsior, Minnesota, as bishop on 11 April 1910. By 1909 the diocese counted 11,000 white and 6,500 Indian Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgical-us:
Bread in the liturgy is chiefly the bread of the Eucharist, consecrated at the altar as Christ consecrated bread at the Last Supper. Whether Christ used leavened or unleavened bread is still debated, since John's Gospel and the other Gospels point different ways, and early practice likely used whatever bread lay at hand.

Customs hardened by region: Eastern churches mostly kept leavened bread, while Western churches chose unleavened. The gap fed sharp dispute at the schism, though either kind counts as valid matter. Early faithful brought their own bread and wine to the altar, a custom echoed when a new bishop offers two loaves, one gilded and one silvered, at his consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-aikenhea:
Mary Aikenhead was foundress of the Irish Sisters of Charity, born at Cork in 1787 and dead at Dublin in 1858. 

Accustomed to active charity and feeling called to religious life, she found no order for outside charitable work. Archbishop Murray chose her against her will to found Ireland's Sisters of Charity. She made a three-year novitiate from 1812 to 1815 at York's Micklegate Bar convent, taking the name Sister Mary Augustine, though the world knew her as Mrs Aikenhead. On 1 September 1815 the first members vowed, with her as superior-general. Sixteen years of organising spread the work through hospitals and rescue work. Shattered health made her an invalid in 1831, yet she directed sisters through the 1832 plague, opened new houses, and sent missions to France and Australia, leaving ten institutions flourishing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monad:
Monad means an ultimate, indivisible unit. This entry follows the word from Greek philosophy through Leibniz, for whom it became the keystone of his system. Pythagoras used it for the unity behind all number. Plato's dialogues used its plural for the Ideas. Aristotle treated it as the principle of number itself, without size and unchanging.

Later thinkers stretched it further. Neoplatonists called God the Monad of Monads. Bruno used it for the tiny substances making up reality. Leibniz built his whole account of substance on it. Each monad mirrors the universe with more or less clarity, from bare attraction in minerals up to intellect in the human soul. God harmonised them all in advance, so no monad truly acts on another.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-office-of-the:
The Office of the Dead, in the Roman liturgy, joins First Vespers, Mass, Matins, and Lauds into one long vigil for the departed. Its Vespers sing psalms 114, 119, 120, 129, and 137 with the Magnificat, its Matins hold three nocturns of psalms and lessons, and Lauds close with the Benedictus.

Unlike other offices it lacks Little Hours, Second Vespers, and Compline, and drops introductions, hymns, and doxologies, recalling ancient vigils that ran from evening through night to dawn. Psalms were chosen for verses that speak of death, and the entry explains each part. The psalms were picked for verses that hint at the state of the dead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prayers-for-t:
Catholic teaching on prayer for the dead is bound to purgatory and to the communion of saints, an article of the Apostles' Creed. Trent's twenty fifth session defined that purgatory is real, and that souls held there are aided by the suffrages of the faithful, above all by the worthy sacrifice of the altar. That line but sums old teaching.

There the truly penitent who die in God's love ere they have paid by worthy fruits of penance for sins done and left undone are cleansed by purgatorial pains after death. The living ease them by Masses, prayers, alms, and other pious offices. Objectors cite Ecclesiastes on the fallen tree lying where it falls. The line likely but pictures the iron rule of nature in this seen world. Even read of the soul's fate, it says at most that heaven or hell is fixed at death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fothad:
Fothad of the Canon, monk of Fahan-Mura, won Irish clergy lasting freedom from military service with a rhymed legal plea. Bard, counsellor, and tutor to Aedh Oirnidh, high king from 794 to 818, he accompanied the king's expedition against Leinster in 804 and obtained exemption of clergy forever from soldiering. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places him at the close of the eighth century.

His gifts stood so high that Aengus submitted his Felire for Fothad's approval. In return Fothad gave Aengus his Remonstrance to King Aedh, protesting conscription of churchmen. That rhymed judicial opinion, known as a canon or decree, gave him his surname na Canoine. It opens: The Church of the living God let her alone, waste her not. The entry preserves a poet whose verse changed law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-willehad:
Willehad, bishop of Bremen, evangelised Frisia and Saxony between the Weser and the Elbe. Born in Northumberland before 745, friend of Alcuin and probably schooled at York under Egbert, he was sent to Frisia between 765 and 774 with King Alchred's leave. He cannot have been Boniface's disciple, as Baronius claims, since Boniface left England in 718 and died in 754.

At Dockum, where Boniface was martyred, he made many converts. He crossed the Lauwers with little success at Hugmarke, then worked at Drenthe. In 780 Charlemagne sent him to Wigmodia near the North Sea, where he built many churches. The Saxon rising under Widukind in 782 killed companions and destroyed churches, and Willehad fled to Rome. Returning, he became Bremen's first bishop. He died at Blexen on 8 November 789.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-wh:
Thomas Whitbread, alias Harcourt, was a Jesuit provincial executed at Tyburn in June 1679 as a victim of the Popish Plot scare. Born in Essex in 1618, he studied at St-Omer, joined the Jesuits in 1635. Worked on the English mission for more than thirty years, mostly in the eastern counties, rising to provincial in 1678.

In that office he had refused to admit Titus Oates to the Society, and Oates soon fabricated his plot. Whitbread was arrested in London on Michaelmas Day 1678, though illness kept him from Newgate for three months. A first indictment collapsed, but a second trial convicted him with four fellow Jesuits on the perjured testimony of Oates, Bedloe, and Dugdale. He also wrote a devotional work and two short poems.
david-s-little-lad:
A Welsh mine story, told by a girl named Gwladys, fills L. T. Meade's tale of 1877. She calls it the story within the story. The papers, she says, were full of the noble deed done by a few Welsh miners, but the heart history of those ten days is known only at home.

The tale opens in September 1876, in an old nursery above the sea. Gwladys asks her nurse Gwen what it is to be buried alive. A mine rescue stands behind the question, and Squire Morgan and her brother pledge that the pit will be made snug and safe. A miner father pulls his front lock and thanks the young lady. Meade writes pathos for young readers, in a Welsh setting.
dialogues-of-the-dead:
Talks among the great dead fill Lord Lyttelton's Dialogues of the Dead, copied here from the Cassell and Company edition of 1889. An introduction tells his life: born in 1709 at Hagley, bred at Eton and Christchurch, Oxford, and raised to the peerage in 1757 after posts that included Chancellor of the Exchequer.

The dialogues first came out in 1760 and were revised for a fourth edition in 1765. Kings, poets, and statesmen of past ages meet and argue in them. One speaker tells how he gave way to some demands of the Commons, yet held back for fear of weakening royal power and the balance of a mixed government. The talks are grave, polite, and full of the age's politics.
doe-osti-17171710-a-first-look-at-backgr:
Amelia Sandoval of Los Alamos takes a first look at background particle hits for a planned silicon tracker at the future Electron Ion Collider, in a report issued 10 August 2026. The collider will smash polarized electrons into heavy ions to probe proton mass, spin, and gluon matter. Its ePIC detector system needs a fast tracker, called the Fast MAPS Tracker, to sort real events from background such as synchrotron radiation.

The tracker aims at 2 nanosecond timing, faster than the 10.2 nanosecond bunch spacing, with top tier spatial precision. Since the new tracker is not yet in the simulations, background files were read through two stand in detectors, a forward gaseous detector and the B0 tracker. Hit distributions from the standard 2 microsecond window will be scaled to the tracker's own window.
doe-osti-2589492-solar-panel-anti-soilin:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory final report NREL/TP-5K00-96625 closes cooperative project CRD-21-17857 with Pellucere Technologies. Technical contact Matthew Muller covers tests of an anti-soiling coating for solar panels. Dust buildup steals output from panels, especially in desert regions, and coatings promise to slow that loss.

Coated glass was built into small test modules with silicon cells and run in a laboratory dust chamber set to mimic desert Southwest sites. Mean humidity across three chamber runs was 44.3 percent. Photos after the runs show the coated module looking clean beside a visibly dusted uncoated module. Field data from a working array compared coated and uncoated panels side by side. The filing gives buyers and plant operators measured soiling rates for both settings.
doe-osti-2997455-baseband-digital-networ:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229011-2025-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-146, by Samson Mai, Arshdeep Singh, Geetha Narayan, and co-authors, upgrades a tuning instrument built into radio-frequency controllers. A digital network analyzer injects a swept chirp signal into a feedback loop and reads the response, revealing gain, phase margin, and delay. Controllers for the Electron-Ion Collider are the long-term home; the running RHIC collider is the test bed.

The analyzer is built on a programmable chip paired with converters, works at baseband, and hands data to a Linux machine where Python scripts compute magnitude and phase. Bench tests compared it against a standard vector network analyzer and used it to tune a one-turn delay feedback loop against a cavity simulator. It also characterized a real RHIC 28 megahertz cavity during an accelerator physics experiment.
doe-osti-3000483-assessment-of-benefits-:
Isabella van Rooyen, Kenneth Ross, Carolyne Burns and co-workers at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory assess solid-state manufacturing for nuclear products in this September 2025 report, M3CR-22PN0402024. Most metal 3D printing melts powder layer by layer, which can leave pores and coarse grains. Solid-state routes knead and bond material without melting it, refining the grain structure as they go, a natural fit for reactor parts that must survive heat and radiation.

The study centres on 316 stainless steel and oxide dispersion strengthened steels, alloys peppered with tiny oxide particles for strength. Benefits claimed for solid-phase processing include finer, more even microstructure, better properties, and lower cost at scale. Bypassing specialist dispersoid powders could simplify supply, since parts form more directly. The report maps where such methods fit the nuclear industry, weighs them against liquid-based printing, and recommends where the Advanced Materials program should push next.
doe-osti-3015358-epcape-stratiform-cloud:
DOE/SC-ARM-26-005, dated January 2026, reports the SCARPE field campaign. Dan Lubin of Scripps Institution of Oceanography wrote it. The campaign measured stratiform cloud radiative properties. The work rode on the Eastern Pacific Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment. It deployed the CC-RIDER radiometer package on the ARM Mobile Facility at Mount Soledad.

CC-RIDER pairs a primary pyranometer with a near-infrared filtered unit and a precision infrared radiometer. Downwelling shortwave and longwave irradiance can thus be split into parts. Those parts respond to liquid water path and droplet size. The filtered channel ties to droplet effective radius. Its band logic sits near 340 to 350 nanometers, where ozone absorption matters little. May 2023 examples and an October 2024 calibration table anchor the short campaign report.
doe-osti-3018128-cost-competitive-proces:
Ali Abouimrane of Oak Ridge National Laboratory is the byline author of this December 2025 CRADA final report, ORNL/TM-2026/4411, for agreement NFE-25-10935 with Nth Cycle Inc. Megan O'Connor, the company's chief executive, certified the report in January 2026. The project developed a cost-competitive process to make battery-grade oxides from aged lithium-ion batteries, closing the loop on old cells.

The work started from precursor cathode material recovered from spent batteries. Measurements confirmed two precursor batches sat close to the NMC811 composition, at nickel 0.82, manganese 0.08, cobalt 0.10 in one case. The team then relithiated the material to restore what age had stripped out. Electrochemical testing showed performance similar to off-the-shelf battery materials. For recyclers, that is the whole business case: yesterday's battery, reborn as feedstock good enough for tomorrow's.
doe-osti-3022674-high-intensity-gamma-ra:
LANL report LA-UR-26-21197, by David Moir and nine colleagues, reports radiography experiments at the High Intensity Gamma-Ray Source. The tests show how image plates perform as detectors for high-energy gamma radiography. The practical question is detector choice: a tantalum converter screen in front of the plate boosts signal, but costs sharpness.

Measurements across energies quantify the trade. At 8 MeV the bare image plate is about seven times less sensitive than the screen-and-plate combination, while delivering roughly twice the resolution at the same energy. Signal without the screen is smooth and consistent across energies. Polynomial fits to the data extract the screen's gain as a function of energy. They confirm the familiar pattern that the screen's benefit grows as gamma energy rises.
doe-osti-3024716-resstock-measure-docume:
Yingli Lou, Rajendra Adhikari, and Andrew Parker of the National Laboratory of the Rockies document an HVAC load flexibility measure for ResStock in report NLR/TP-5500-93846, dated March 2026. ResStock simulates the national housing stock house by house. This measure models thermostats that shift heating and cooling load away from peak hours, a cheap source of grid flexibility hiding in ordinary homes.

The measure's inputs define the scenario: a pre-peak period and thermostat set point offsets, applied over on-peak hours that are tabulated separately for summer, winter, and intermediate months. One rule is spelled out for edge cases: if a home's baseline schedule already sits in a setback or setup state, the flexibility change still applies. Diagrams show the modeling approach, and the documentation fixes exactly how the measure behaves so studies using it can be reproduced.
doe-osti-3179919-deformation-of-nano-met:
Wendy Gu of Stanford University reports under award DE-SC0021075, dated April 30, 2026, on a new way to study how metals bend and crack. Metallic glasses are strong, hard, and resist corrosion and wear, which suits them for implants and microgears. Yet how they deform stays mysterious, because standard samples give researchers no knobs to tune the inner structure that controls the behavior.

The project made nano-metallic glasses by colloidal synthesis, a chemistry route that freezes in structures far from equilibrium. These tiny glasses also bend more than expected, a trait worth copying by design. Side work covered gold bi-crystals with Sandia, thin magnetic films, and lithium metal battery parts. In those cells, lithium dendrites can pierce the solid electrolyte and short the battery, and the team probed where the spikes start.
doe-osti-3364477-a-framework-for-streaml:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38441, by Devyn Powell, Shahnawaz Siddiqui, Jessica Kerby, Alan Cooke, Sara Murphy, and Thomas Benson, dates to September 2025. It assesses how large electric loads connect to the grid and how the process could run faster without losing fairness. Connection studies and upgrade bills now shape whether data centers and factories get built at all.

Current practice varies widely by utility, and cost allocation is the sharpest dispute. Portland General Electric proposed lower upgrade charges for customers with flat, stable demand, arguing they benefit the system. In Texas, ERCOT uses refundable deposits so serious developers fund studies while canceled projects are not punished. The framework collects such strategies into a checklist for utilities and regulators redesigning their queues.
doe-osti-3375599-final-technical-report-:
Final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0021359 closes the U.S.-Japan Hadronic Physics Exchange Program at the University of Connecticut. Kyungseon Joo led the program as principal investigator. The subject field is hadron structure and quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force. The program paid for U.S. scientists to work at Japanese labs, and built ties the other way as well. It ties into the 2023 DOE and NSF long-range plan for nuclear physics.

The report lists exchange visits year by year. UConn and George Washington staff spent weeks at Osaka University in 2023 and 2024. Others worked at the J-PARC accelerator site with host H. Sako. One visitor went to Tohoku University in 2021. The program frames these stays as workforce growth as much as research. Young scientists gain time on foreign gear and inside foreign groups, then bring those links home.
doe-osti-3377979-initial-feasibility-ass:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4625, dated June 2026, assesses the feasibility of integrating fibers into parts during advanced manufacturing. Four authors are printed: Holden C. Hyer, Joshua Kendall, Anthony Birri, and Christian M. Petrie. The opening frames the motive as structural health monitoring, watching a part's condition from inside rather than inspecting it from outside.

Embedding a fiber, such as an optical sensing fiber, while a part is being built could let the finished component report strain or temperature for its whole service life. The report pairs an initial feasibility assessment with broader strategy development, asking both whether the integration can be done and how a program should pursue it. It is an early-stage planning document rather than a test report.
five-little-peppers-abroad:
Margaret Sidney's Five Little Peppers Abroad takes the Pepper family over the ocean, after readers begged for more of their good times. Friends of the family had pressed Sidney for the stories Polly told in the little brown house, and for the plays and exploits that the main series could not hold.

This volume answers a further pressure: a book showing the Little Peppers abroad, where their family life, humour and mutual care meet new scenes. Fanny Y. Cory's illustrations accompany the text. Readers who grew up with the Peppers will enjoy travelling with them again, and new readers will find a warm, old-fashioned family story.
further-adventures-of-lad:
Albert Payson Terhune returned to his collie Lad in Further Adventures of Lad, a second book of tales from Sunnybank, his New Jersey homestead. Terhune's foreword reports that the first Lad book won the old dog a million friends, and that seventeen hundred visitors had come to see Lad's grave. Most of these stories first ran, shortened, in the Ladies' Home Journal.

The tales follow Lad guarding the Place against burglars, tracking, stowing away, and facing intruders, with chapter titles like Hero-Stuff and No Trespassing. Terhune insists the incidents are true and the telling clumsy, a pose his readers loved. Anyone who wants the classic American dog story, sentimental, brave, and country-house cozy, will find Lad in fine form here.
garthowen-a-story-of-a-welsh-homestead:
Allen Raine sets her novel at a Welsh farm called Garthowen, in a seaport town in South Wales. Sailor Gethin Owens comes home to the world of his youth, where his kin farm the slopes above the sea. Chapters bear names like Morva of the Moor, The Old Bible, and Sara's Vision. Raine wrote other Welsh tales, among them Torn Sails and By Berwen Banks.

Love, faith, and family pull at the folk of the farm. Gwenda's hopes, Gethin's past at sea, and a strict chapel home all shape the plot. Scenes move from lodging-house teas to dances on the cliffs. Welsh speech and song run through the talk. The book gives a warm, close picture of rural Welsh life, its joys, and its hard rules.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OurDailyBread_O:
The January 7, 1966 issue of 'The Poultryman' is a trade newspaper for the poultry industry. Its lead story reports a new broiler house built by Allen's Hatchery of Seaford, Delaware. The house held 108,000 birds. Around that story, the issue carries the ordinary traffic of an industry paper: prices, equipment, and farm news.

Trade papers like this one were the trade's memory of itself. A 108,000-bird house was news in 1966 because it marked the scale farming was reaching. The issue survives in assassination files for reasons of filing rather than content. For readers, it is a clean sample of a farm trade weekly at work, chicken economics reported straight.
java-head:
Joseph Hergesheimer published Java Head in 1918, a novel of Salem shipping folk. Laurel Ammidon has just turned eleven as the book opens, lying in bed at dawn. She gives up her fancy that chairs have life and character, with some melancholy. Chairs are chairs, she now tells herself, things to sit on.

A Batavia beau of fifty with a bald head and smirking bow woos in a later social scene. Roger Brevard leads Sidsall to a garden door as cloud veils the sun. Old China trade wealth, family pride, and a Javanese wife's shadow hang over the Ammidons.
joseph-conrad:
Hugh Walpole's Joseph Conrad is a short study of the novelist, published at New York in 1916. Walpole dedicates the book to Sir Sidney Colvin, in friendship. Four parts make up the study: Biography, The Novelist, The Poet, and Romance and Realism. A short bibliography and an American bibliography follow, with an index.

That plan shows Walpole's aim: first the seaman's life, then the maker of novels judged as artist. Treating Conrad as a poet sets this study apart from plain life stories. The romance and realism chapter weighs the two strains in Conrad's sea tales and novels of adventure. Written while Conrad still lived, it is an early act of criticism by a younger novelist.
my-three-days-in-gilead: Elmer U. Hoenshel wrote My Three Days in Gilead, a title that points to the biblical land of Gilead. The hosted sample preserves only the Project Gutenberg file header, with no readable book text at all. No title page, preface, or chapter text survives in the sample. For that reason the book's journey, scenes, and claims cannot be described from the hosted evidence, and only its title and author can be stated with confidence.
nasa-tm-19680012262-calculations-of-non-:
James K. Harrison, at the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama, calculates lunar heat glow in this memorandum. He asks how much infrared radiation from the Moon's surface falls on a small flat plate hovering just above it. The plate's height and tilt both vary in the study.

The Moon's surface does not radiate evenly in all directions, and Harrison assumes that non-diffuse behavior. His calculations compare that realistic case with a perfectly diffuse surface. The heat falling on the plate, he finds, can differ significantly between the two. Landers and hovering instruments needed that difference to predict their own heating.
secret-bread:
F. Tennyson Jesse published this novel with George H. Doran in New York in 1917. Jesse had earlier written The Milky Way and Beggars on Horseback. A short line from Proverbs about bread eaten in secret gives the book its name and its theme.

Book One, called Sowing, opens with high adventure in a farmyard, then moves through a mill, a kitchen, and chapel scenes. A boy grows up amid farm work, faith, and strong feeling on the moor. Jesse builds a slow, close study of a young life and the hidden hopes that shape it.
songs-merry-and-sad: John Charles McNeill, an American poet of North Carolina who lived from 1874 to 1907, wrote Songs, Merry and Sad. He gives the book to Joseph P. Caldwell, called the Old Man. The contents open with The Bride, Oh, Ask Me Not, Isabel, and a piece for Jane's birthday. A Secret, The Old Bad Woman, Valentine, and A Photograph follow, and later heads name home songs, an Easter hymn, a Christmas hymn, and When I Go Home.
tales-of-the-road: Charles N. Crewdson wrote Tales of the Road in 1905, with art by J. J. Gould, and gave the book to Alex C. Ritchey, a salesman and his friend. Eighteen parts cover the work of traveling salesmen, from The Square Deal Wins and Tricks of the Trade to Tactics in Selling, Cutting Prices, Canceled Orders, and Hearts Behind the Order Book.
the-adventures-of-old-mr-toad: Thornton W. Burgess wrote The Adventures of Old Mr. Toad, with art by Harrison Cady, in 1920, a Smiling Pool tale in twenty-three chapters. Heads track Jimmy Skunk's puzzle, a hunt for Old Mr. Toad, his music bag and queer tongue, a shadow over the pool, his babies at the pool kindergarten, and a lesson learned at the close.
the-altar-of-the-dead:
Henry James wrote this long story, shown here in a London edition from Martin Secker first issued in 1916 and set from the Definitive Edition text. Its main figure, Stransom, has kept one date sacred for years: the day Mary Antrim died. She was to have been his wife, but a harsh fever took her after the wedding day had been set.

Grief rules Stransom's house and habits long after that loss. He has done much in the world, the opening says, except one thing: he has never forgotten her. Memory acts like a priestless altar in his life, and each year the date takes hold of him anew.
the-broken-road: A. E. W. Mason wrote The Broken Road, dated 1907. Mason had also written Four Feathers, The Truants, and Running Water. The chapters start with The Breaking of the Road and Inside the Fort. Linforth's Death and Luffe Looks Forward come next. A Magazine Article, A Long Walk, and In the Dauphiné lead to A String of Pearls. The Invidious Bar, Shere Ali meeting an old friend, News from Mecca, and Sybil Linforth's Loyalty fill the late list. A Gift Misunderstood is the last head shown.
the-cockaynes-in-paris-or-gone-abroad:
Blanchard Jerrold wrote this comic account of the English abroad, with sketches by Gustave Dore and other pictures drawn from a French point of view. John Camden Hotten published it in London at Piccadilly. A picture caption shows Mi Lord Anglais at Mabille, smiling and splendid, at ease among French dancers.

Jerrold's preface looks back with mixed feelings. The Cockaynes' story was written some years earlier, when Paris stood at her best and brightest, the English quarter was crowded, and the Emperor was at St. Cloud. France then seemed set to become the richest and strongest country in the world. Where the Cockaynes carried guide-books and opera-glasses into raptures, dismal ruins now stand. The Vendome Column is a stump, wreathed with a huge immortelle and capped with the tricolor.
the-copyright-question-a-letter-to-the-t:
George N. Morang of Toronto published The Copyright Question in 1902 as a letter to the secretary of the Toronto Board of Trade, dated February 19 of that year. The board's council had backed a plan drawn from a bill proposed in 1895 by Mr. Hall Caine.

Under that plan, a book would have to be printed and bound in Canada to gain Canadian copyright, and stay in Canadian print to keep it. If a book were not printed in Canada within a fair time, the government could license a Canadian publisher to print it, with safeguards giving the owner a fair royalty. Morang traces the plan to talks in 1895 between Caine, speaking for English authors, Mr. Daldy for English publishers, and Canadian publishers, papermakers, printers, and bookbinders.
the-dawn-of-canadian-history-a-chronicle:
Stephen Leacock wrote The Dawn of Canadian History as part of the Chronicles of Canada, a set in thirty-two volumes edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton, printed at Toronto in 1915. His contents run from Before the Dawn and Man in America through the aborigines of Canada, the legend of the Norsemen, and the Bristol voyages, closing with a note on sources.

Chapter I grants that Canada is a new country in one sense: European settlement there goes back only three hundred years. Its written history is a little span beside the long annals of Europe and the East. In another sense, he argues, part of it may be the oldest country in the world. The planet itself began, on the nebular theory, as a fiery molten mass cooling into the globe we know.
the-golden-road:
L. M. Montgomery wrote The Golden Road. She dedicates the book to the memory of Aunt Mary Lawson. Aunt Mary told her many of the tales the Story Girl repeats. A foreword looks back at youth as a road. The road runs through the Land of Lost Delight. Shadow and sunshine were sweetly mixed there.

Chapter I is called A New Departure. It opens on a wild November night. The young folk sit in a half-circle round a wood fire. The fire burns in Uncle Alec's kitchen. The narrator says he has thought of something amusing for the winter. The foreword frames the tales to come. They are a keepsake of the golden road of youth. Those memories, Montgomery says, are among the dearest things a person owns.
the-history-of-a-mouthful-of-bread:
Jean Mace wrote The History of a Mouthful of Bread, on the effect of food on the organization of men and animals. The book was translated from the eighth French edition by Mrs. Alfred Gatty. Extracts from the preface to the English edition note that the University Commission at Paris adopted the volume among its prize books.

Gatty admits she began with doubt that the subject suited young people, then became a firm convert to the author's views. The book speaks in letters to a child, at first to a little girl. Difficult facts of science are set out with quaint, droll comparisons meant to win smiles while the lesson lands.
the-iliad: Homer's Iliad appears here in English prose, done by Andrew Lang, Walter Leaf, and Ernest Meyers, fellows respectively of Merton College, Oxford, Trinity College, Cambridge, and Wadham College, Oxford. Macmillan published this revised edition in London in 1911. Only the title page and the contents are present here, so the translation itself does not appear. The contents run from a prefatory note through the books of the poem in sequence, laying out the whole architecture of the epic of Achilles and the Trojan War in bare headings.
the-innocents-abroad: Mark Twain's Innocents Abroad is drawn here from the 1869 first edition. Only the contents are present in this record. The travel narrative itself does not appear. The chapter summaries read like jokes in miniature. The excursion's programme opens them. The celebrities defect at once. Horse-billiards and a synagogue enliven the sea days. Mr. Blucher gives his opinions. A fossil community waits in the Azores. The Pillars of Hercules follow. A private frolic in Africa closes the list shown. It beards a Moorish garrison without loss of life.
the-jericho-road: W. Bion Adkins wrote this little book for the Odd Fellows. He also wrote Twelve Steps Toward Heaven. The book appeared in 1901. He dedicated it to his worthy and gentle brothers. He hoped it would spur greater effort for the beloved order. An opening comparison sets the theme. Rivers run forever yet are never passed. Winds go forever yet are never gone. Odd-Fellowship is like both. Only the dedication and motto pages are present here. The body of the book does not appear.
the-leicestershires-beyond-baghdad: Edward J. Thompson, holder of the Military Cross, wrote a First World War account of his regiment service beyond Baghdad. Only the title page and publication details of the first edition, issued by the Epworth Press in London, are present here. Thompson other books named on the page include Mesopotamian verses and Ennerdale Bridge. The narrative of the Leicestershire regiment march and fighting in Mesopotamia is absent from this record beyond that title page.
the-lost-road:
The Lost Road gathers ten novels and stories by Richard Harding Davis. Among them are The Miracle of Las Palmas, The Men of Zanzibar, The Long Arm, The Buried Treasure of Cobre, and Somewhere in France. An introduction by John T. McCutcheon, titled With Davis in Vera Cruz, Brussels, and Salonika, is part memorial. McCutcheon finds it hard to realize that Davis has covered his last story and will not be seen again among the men who follow the war game.

He calls it bitter irony that Davis was torn away in the middle of the greatest event of all, with the story unfinished. Yet Davis left at the flood tide, McCutcheon writes, still supreme as the best reporter in his country. The collection thus reads as both fiction and tribute to a famous correspondent.
the-old-gray-homestead:
Frances Parkinson Keyes published The Old Gray Homestead in 1919 and dedicated it to the farm families who had been her neighbors for fifteen years. She calls it a quiet story of a farm. The first chapter opens on a hot April day, with Sally Gray driving home from teaching school with her brother Austin.

Austin is lean, dark, and bitter, worn down by farm hardship, while Sally is plain, plump, and calm. She wishes he could find money, love, or some encouragement. Keyes builds the tale on close knowledge of country people, their talk, their mud, their weather, and their hopes.
the-old-homestead:
Mrs. Ann S. Stephens wrote The Old Homestead, a story of New England farm life. Stephens was a prolific novelist, author of Fashion and Famine, The Heiress, and many other tales listed on the title page. A publisher's notice praises her plots, her knowledge of human nature, and her young lovers and their trials.

The first chapter, The Father's Return, opens with a child kneeling by a pauper bed and wondering if he will come. Stephens mixes pathos with home and fireside feeling. The notice promises an absorbing plot and characters true to nature, in the popular vein of farm-life fiction and stage plays of the day.
the-purple-land-being-the-narrative-of-o:
W. H. Hudson tells, through narrator Richard Lamb, of adventures in the Banda Oriental in South America, in a second edition of 1904 illustrated by Keith Henderson. Hudson's preface recalls the first issue of 1885 under the longer title naming the purple land that England lost.

That first edition drew few and mostly unkind notices, was shelved as travel, and soon vanished. Friendly men of letters rescued it, and Hudson revised wording throughout and cut passages for the reprint. Readers get both an adventure narrative and an unusually frank account of an author's first book failing and returning.
the-secret-chamber-at-chad:
Everett Evelyn-Green's The Secret Chamber at Chad opens with a mysterious visitor, according to its contents. Later chapters name the household at Chad and Brother Emmanuel. A travelling preacher, a warning, and a search follow. From peril to safety closes the list of ten chapters.

Chapter one shows the great house wrapped in sleep. June moonlight strikes its gray masonry with strong white light. Castellated turrets and twisted chimneys stand out against a pine wood. Chad had been shorn of glory during the Wars of the Roses, the narrator explains. One of its two quadrangles lay in ruins and was never rebuilt. The seventh Henry now sits on the throne. Bosworth Field ended the strife between York and Lancaster, and the household rejoices in the peace.
the-texan-scouts-a-story-of-the-alamo-an: Joseph A. Altsheler's Texan Scouts, a story of the Alamo and Goliad dated 1913, continues the fortunes of Ned Fulton from The Texan Star, as its own note explains. The pages present here stop at the title and the first contents entries. Those entries open in a storm, move to captives and a fight with Urrea, and arrive at Santa Anna's advance and the Alamo itself. Readers can see the historical ground the novel covers, while Altsheler's battle narrative remains beyond this record.
the-tin-woodman-of-oz-a-faithful-story-o:
L. Frank Baum's Tin Woodman of Oz is dedicated to his grandson Frank Alden Baum and introduced by the author's own letter to readers. Baum says correspondents kept asking what became of the pretty Munchkin girl Nick Chopper meant to wed, before the Wicked Witch's spell on his axe. He wondered himself, he admits, until Woot the Wanderer took up the matter. The Tin Woodman has now found her, after many thrilling adventures.

Baum shares letters showing readers from a boy of five to a married couple past seventy, all eager for Oz. His questioner, a college professor, wanted to know what age his books suit. Baum's answer is the whole audience. The quest that follows, with the Scarecrow and Polychrome helping, settles one of the oldest loose ends in the Oz series.
tom-sawyer-abroad:
Mark Twain lets Huck Finn ask whether Tom Sawyer could stay satisfied after their river adventures and Jim's freeing. Fame only poisoned Tom for more, Huck says. The village gave them a torchlight procession, and boys knuckled to Tom Sawyer the Traveler.

Old Nat Parsons, the postmaster and the village's only rival traveller for thirty years, threatens Tom's glory. Contents promise a balloon ascension, storms, a caravan, a disappearing lake, treasure hill, and a sandstorm across thirteen chapters. Readers get Huck's voice narrating Tom's hunger for adventure, now pointed at Africa by balloon.
under-fire-the-story-of-a-squad: Henri Barbusse's Under Fire, the story of a squad, was translated by Fitzwater Wray. Barbusse dedicates the book to comrades who fell beside him at Crouy and on Hill 119 in 1915. The contents list twenty-four chapters, from The Vision and In the Earth to bombardment, the chapter called Under Fire, and The Dawn. Only the dedication and contents are present here, so the squad's story itself does not appear.
unleavened-bread:
Robert Grant published Unleavened Bread with Charles Scribner's Sons at New York in 1900. The novel stands in three books whose titles chart a life: The Emancipation, The Struggle, and The Success. Chapter one opens as wedding guests leave a country house on a bright September night, driving off in hay carts with songs and laughter floating back down the road.

Among the last to leave are Babcock and Selma White. Selma rides home in a chaise, well wrapped against the autumn air, in no hurry over the seven miles. Festive nights and the open devotion of a city young man are new things in her quiet life, though she has always been treated with care. Grant sets her at a turning point: a woman used to being tacitly placed first in her small world, now facing a wider one.
where-angels-fear-to-tread:
E. M. Forster opens Where Angels Fear to Tread at Charing Cross station in London. A crowd has come to see Lilia Herriton off to Italy. Her brother-in-law Philip, her mother-in-law, and small Irma all crowd the platform. Lilia laughs without pause at the fuss and calls it an ovation fit for royalty.

Philip pours out last advice on where to stop and how to learn Italian. He urges her to leave the track, see small towns like Gubbio and Cortona, and love the Italian people. Italy, he says, is no mere museum of old art. Forster's first novel turns a widow's trip into love, scandal, and clash of English and Italian ways.
willis-the-pilot-a-sequel-to-the-swiss-f:
Willis the Pilot continues the tale of the Swiss Family Robinson, as its preface explains. Lee and Shepard printed the book in Boston in 1875. The preface retells the source story: a Swiss clergyman sailed with his wife and four sons for a Pacific island. A storm drove their ship off course near New Guinea and wrecked it on an unknown coast.

Youth in the present day, the preface says, loves adventure and tales of new lands. That taste keeps the Robinson book popular with old and young alike. The sequel adds a pilot named Willis and new travels for the castaway family. Sea peril, natural history, and tales fill the pages. Castaway adventure drives the book.
